Choice A is the best answer. The convention being tested is the use of finite verbs in a relative clause. Relative clauses, such as the one beginning with “which,” require a finite verb, a verb that can function as the main verb of a clause. This choice correctly supplies the clause with the finite past tense verb “provided.”

Choice B is incorrect because the non-finite participle “having provided” doesn’t supply the clause with a finite verb. Choice C is incorrect because the non-finite to-infinitive “to provide” doesn’t supply the clause with a finite verb. Choice D is incorrect because the non-finite participle “providing” doesn’t supply the clause with a finite verb.

question.paragraph: In 1453, English King Henry VI became unfit to rule after falling gravely ill. As a result, Parliament appointed Richard, Third Duke of York, who had a strong claim to the English throne, to rule as Lord Protector. Upon recovering two years later, ______ forcing an angered Richard from the royal court and precipitating a series of battles later known as the Wars of the Roses.
question.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: it was Henry who resumed his reign,
question.explanation:
Choice A is the best answer. The convention being tested is subject-modifier placement. This choice ensures that the introductory phrase “upon recovering two years later” appears immediately before the noun it modifies (“Henry”), clearly establishing that Henry recovered two years later.

Choice B is incorrect because it results in a dangling modifier. The placement of the noun phrase “the reign of Henry” immediately after the introductory phrase illogically suggests that the reign of Henry recovered two years later. Choice C is incorrect because it results in a dangling modifier. The placement of the noun phrase “Henry’s reign” immediately after the introductory phrase illogically suggests that Henry’s reign recovered two years later. Choice D is incorrect because it results in a dangling modifier. The placement of the function word “it” immediately after the introductory phrase illogically suggests that “it” recovered two years later.

question.paragraph: At eight paragraphs long, the preamble to the constitution of ______ country in Western Asia—is much longer than the one-paragraph preamble to the United States Constitution.
question.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
question.explanation:
Choice A is the best answer. The convention being tested is the punctuation of a supplementary element within a sentence. The dash after “Bahrain” pairs with the dash after “Asia” to separate the supplementary element “a country in Western Asia” from the rest of the sentence. 

Choice B is incorrect because a comma can’t be paired with a dash in this way to separate the supplementary element from the rest of the sentence. Choice C is incorrect because it fails to use appropriate punctuation to separate the supplementary element from the rest of the sentence. Choice D is incorrect because a colon can’t be paired with a dash in this way to separate the supplementary element from the rest of the sentence.

question.paragraph: In 1990, California native and researcher Ellen Ochoa left her position as chief of the Intelligent Systems Technology Branch at a NASA research center ______ the space agency’s astronaut training program.
question.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
question.explanation:
Choice A is the best answer. The convention being tested is the use of nonfinite verb forms in a sentence. The nonfinite to-infinitive verb "to join" is correctly used to form a subordinate clause that expresses why Ochoa left her position (to join the training program).

Choice B is incorrect because the finite verb "is joining" can’t be used in this way to indicate Ochoa’s action of joining the training program. A conjunction such as "and" would be needed to coordinate "is joining" with the previous finite verb, "left." Choice C is incorrect because the finite verb "joined" can’t be used in this way to indicate Ochoa’s action of joining the training program. A conjunction such as "and" would be needed to coordinate "joined" with the previous finite verb, "left." Choice D is incorrect because the finite verb "joins" can’t be used in this way to indicate Ochoa’s action of joining the training program. A conjunction such as "and" would be needed to coordinate "joins" with the previous finite verb, "left."

question.paragraph: Why are Rome’s famous concrete structures, such as the Colosseum, still standing after 2,000-plus years, when modern concrete may not even last for fifty? Scientists ______ that the secret to Roman concrete’s durability was its unique blend of ingredients, which included volcanic ash and seawater.
question.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
question.explanation:
Choice A is the best answer. The convention being tested is the use of verb forms within a sentence. The main clause of a sentence requires a finite (tensed) verb, and this choice supplies the finite present tense verb “explain” to indicate what the scientists do.

Choice B is incorrect because it results in an ungrammatical sentence. The nonfinite participle “having explained” doesn’t supply the main clause with a finite verb. Choice C is incorrect because it results in an ungrammatical sentence. The nonfinite participle “explaining” doesn’t supply the main clause with a finite verb. Choice D is incorrect because it results in an ungrammatical sentence. The nonfinite to-infinitive “to explain” doesn’t supply the main clause with a finite verb.

question.paragraph: While many video game creators strive to make their graphics ever more ______ others look to the past, developing titles with visuals inspired by the “8-bit” games of the 1980s and 1990s. (The term “8-bit” refers to a console whose processor could only handle eight bits of data at once.)
question.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
question.explanation:
Choice C is the best answer. The convention being tested is punctuation between a subordinate clause and a main clause. This choice correctly uses a comma to mark the boundary between the subordinate clause (“While…lifelike”) and the main clause (“others look to the past”).

Choice A is incorrect because it results in an incomplete sentence with no main clause. Choice B is incorrect because it fails to mark the boundary between the subordinate clause (“While…lifelike”) and the main clause (“others…past”). Choice D is incorrect because it results in an incomplete sentence with no main clause.

question.paragraph: A model created by biologist Luis Valente predicts that the rate of speciation—the rate at which new species form—on an isolated island located approximately 5,000 kilometers from the nearest mainland ______ triple the rate of speciation on an island only 500 kilometers from the mainland.
question.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
question.explanation:
Choice D is the best answer. The convention being tested is finite and nonfinite verb forms within a sentence. Relative clauses, such as the one beginning with “that,” require a finite verb, a verb that can function as the main verb of a clause. This choice correctly supplies the clause with the finite future tense verb “will be.” 

Choice A is incorrect because the nonfinite participle “being” doesn’t supply the clause with a finite verb. Choice B is incorrect because the nonfinite to-infinitive “to be” doesn’t supply the clause with a finite verb. Choice C is incorrect because the nonfinite to-infinitive “to have been” doesn’t supply the clause with a finite verb.

question.paragraph: For thousands of years, people in the Americas ______ the bottle gourd, a large bitter fruit with a thick rind, to make bottles, other types of containers, and even musical instruments. Oddly, there is no evidence that any type of bottle gourd is native to the Western Hemisphere; either the fruit or its seeds must have somehow been carried from Asia or Africa.
question.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
question.explanation:
Choice B is the best answer. The convention being tested is finite and nonfinite verb forms within a sentence. A main clause requires a finite verb to perform the action of the subject (in this case, “people in the Americas”), and this choice supplies the finite past perfect tense verb “have used” to indicate what people in the Americas used the gourd for. 

Choice A is incorrect because the nonfinite to-infinitive “to use” doesn’t supply the main clause with a finite verb. Choice C is incorrect because the nonfinite participle “having used” doesn’t supply the main clause with a finite verb. Choice D is incorrect because the nonfinite participle “using” doesn’t supply the main clause with a finite verb.

question.paragraph: The 2022 Nobel Prize in Chemistry was awarded to three pioneers in the field of click chemistry: two-time Nobel laureate Barry Sharpless, who coined the term “click chemistry” in 1998; Carolyn Bertozzi, founder of the Bertozzi Group at ______ and Morten Meldal, a professor at the University of Copenhagen in Denmark.
question.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
question.explanation:
Choice D is the best answer. This choice correctly uses a semicolon to punctuate a complex list (which is made up of items that have commas in them).

Choice A is incorrect. This is a complex list, indicated by the semicolon between "1998" and "Carolyn Bertozzi." What comes after the blank is a separate list item, so punctuation is needed after "Stanford." Choice B is incorrect. This is a complex list, indicated by the semicolon between "1998" and "Carolyn Bertozzi." The items in this list have internal punctuation in the form of commas and must therefore be separated by semicolons to avoid confusion. Choice C is incorrect. This is a complex list, indicated by the semicolon between "1998" and "Carolyn Bertozzi." Colons aren’t used to separate items in a list.

question.paragraph: In 1881, French chemist Camille Faure redesigned the rechargeable lead-acid battery. Faure’s design greatly increased the amount of electricity that the original battery, which the French physicist Gaston Planté ______ fifteen years earlier, could hold.
question.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
question.explanation:
Choice D is the best answer. Faure redesigned the battery in 1881, and the original battery was invented “fifteen years earlier.” Notice that this is the only choice in the past tense. To indicate that a past occurrence took place before another past occurrence, we need to use “had” + the past tense form of the verb. This is called the “past perfect” tense.

Choice A is incorrect. This choice creates a tense error. Planté invented the original battery in the past, so we shouldn’t use the present tense “is inventing.” Choice B is incorrect. This choice creates a tense error. Planté invented the original battery in the past, so we shouldn’t use the future tense “will invent.” Choice C is incorrect. This choice creates a tense error. Planté invented the original battery in the past, so we shouldn’t use the present tense “invents.”

question.paragraph: In ancient Greece, an Epicurean was a follower of Epicurus, a philosopher whose beliefs revolved around the pursuit of pleasure. Epicurus defined pleasure as “the absence of pain in the body and of trouble in the ______ that all life’s virtues derived from this absence.
question.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
question.explanation:
Choice A is the best answer. The convention being tested is punctuation use between a main clause and a participial phrase. This choice correctly uses a comma to mark the boundary between the main clause (“Epicurus…‘soul’”) and the participial phrase (“positing…absence”) that provides additional information about how Epicurus defined pleasure.

Choice B is incorrect because a colon can’t be used in this way to join a main clause and a participial phrase. Choice C is incorrect because a semicolon can’t be used in this way to join a main clause and a participial phrase. Choice D is incorrect because it results in a rhetorically unacceptable sentence fragment beginning with “positing.”

question.paragraph: The Alvarez theory, developed in 1980 by physicist Luis Walter Alvarez and his geologist son Walter Alvarez, maintained that the secondary effects of an asteroid impact caused many dinosaurs and other animals to die ______ it left unexplored the question of whether unrelated volcanic activity might have also contributed to the mass extinctions.
question.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
question.explanation:
Choice B is the best answer. The convention being tested is the coordination of main clauses within a sentence. This choice correctly uses a comma and the coordinating conjunction “but” to join the first main clause (“the Alvarez…out”) and the second main clause (“it left…extinctions”).

Choice A is incorrect because when coordinating two longer main clauses such as these, it’s conventional to use a comma before the coordinating conjunction. Choice C is incorrect because it results in a run-on sentence. The two main clauses are fused without punctuation and/or a conjunction. Choice D is incorrect because it results in a comma splice. Without a conjunction following it, a comma can’t be used in this way to join two main clauses.

question.paragraph: A pioneer in the field of taphonomy (the study of how organic remains become fossils), ______ may be just as prevalent in the fossil record as those of thick-shelled organisms.
question.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: fossils of thin-shelled organisms, Anna Behrensmeyer demonstrated in a 2005 analysis,
Anna Behrensmeyer demonstrated in a 2005 analysis that fossils of thin-shelled organisms
it was demonstrated in a 2005 analysis by Anna Behrensmeyer that fossils of thin-shelled organisms
a 2005 analysis—by Anna Behrensmeyer—demonstrated that fossils of thin-shelled organisms
question.explanation:
Choice B is the best answer. The convention being tested is subject-modifier placement. This choice makes the noun phrase “Anna Behrensmeyer” the subject of the sentence and places it immediately after the modifying phrase “a pioneer…fossils.” In doing so, this choice clearly establishes that Anna Behrensmeyer—and not another noun in the sentence—is a pioneer in the field of taphonomy.

Choice A is incorrect because it results in a dangling modifier. The placement of the noun phrase “fossils of thin-shelled organisms” immediately after the modifying phrase illogically suggests that the “fossils” are a pioneer in the field of taphonomy. Choice C is incorrect because it results in a dangling modifier. The placement of the pronoun “it” immediately after the modifying phrase illogically suggests that “it” is a pioneer in the field of taphonomy. Choice D is incorrect because it results in a dangling modifier. The placement of the noun phrase “a 2005 analysis” immediately after the modifying phrase illogically suggests that “a 2005 analysis” is a pioneer in the field of taphonomy.

question.paragraph: Because a cycle of lunar phases ______ 29.5 days to complete, it’s possible to observe two full moons in a single month, one at the beginning and one at the end.
question.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
question.explanation:
Choice D is the best answer. The convention being tested is subject-verb agreement. The singular verb "takes" agrees in number with the singular subject "a cycle of lunar phases."

Choice A is incorrect because the plural verb "are taking" doesn’t agree in number with the singular subject "a cycle of lunar phases." Choice B is incorrect because the plural verb "have taken" doesn’t agree in number with the singular subject "a cycle of lunar phases." Choice C is incorrect because the plural verb "take" doesn’t agree in number with the singular subject "a cycle of lunar phases."

question.paragraph: The alga species Chlorella vulgaris is very efficient at making oxygen. For this reason, scientists are currently exploring ways to use this species in space. C. vulgaris might be used, for example, to build future biological air exchange systems that ______ oxygen for astronauts.
question.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
question.explanation:
Choice C is the best answer. The convention being tested is the use of verbs to express tense. Simple present tense verbs can be used to describe actions that tend to occur, including in a hypothetical or future scenario. In this case, the simple present tense verb “produce” indicates what the air exchange systems might be able to do in the future (produce oxygen for astronauts).

Choice A is incorrect. The present progressive tense verb “are producing” suggests that the oxygen is currently being produced, not that it might be produced in the future. Choice B is incorrect because the past tense verb “produced” suggests that the oxygen was produced in the past, not that it might be produced in the future. Choice D is incorrect because the present perfect tense verb “have produced” suggests that the oxygen has been produced from a point in the past up to the present, not that it might be produced in the future.

question.paragraph: With its towering, six-spired exterior of granitelike quartz monzonite, the Salt Lake Temple is one of the most instantly recognizable structures in the state of Utah. However, many people do not know that ______ built over the course of forty years, with construction beginning in 1853 and ending in 1893.
question.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
question.explanation:
Choice A is the best answer. The convention being tested is pronoun-antecedent agreement. The singular pronoun "it" agrees in number with the singular antecedent "the Salt Lake Temple."

Choice B is incorrect because the singular pronoun "one" is ambiguous in this context; the resulting sentence leaves unclear whether there is only one Salt Lake temple or multiple. Choice C is incorrect because the plural pronoun "they" doesn’t agree in number with the singular antecedent "the Salt Lake Temple." Choice D is incorrect because the plural pronoun "both" doesn’t agree in number with the singular antecedent "the Salt Lake Temple."

question.paragraph: In her analysis of Edith Wharton’s The House of Mirth (1905), scholar Candace Waid observes that the novel depicts the upper classes of New York society as “consumed by the appetite of a soulless ______ an apt assessment given that The House of Mirth is set during the Gilded Age, a period marked by rapid industrialization, economic greed, and widening wealth disparities.
question.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
question.explanation:
Choice C is the best answer. The convention being tested is punctuation between a main clause and a supplementary noun phrase. This choice correctly uses a comma to mark the boundary between the main clause (“scholar…materialism”) and the supplementary noun phrase (“an apt assessment”) that describes Waid’s observation about how The House of Mirth depicts the upper classes of New York society.

Choice A is incorrect because a semicolon and the conjunction “and” can’t be used in this way to mark the boundary between a main clause and a supplementary noun phrase. Choice B is incorrect. Joining the main clause (“scholar…materialism”) and the following noun phrase with the conjunction “and” results in a confusing and illogical sentence that suggests that the novel depicts the upper classes of New York society as “an apt assessment,” which doesn’t make sense in this context. Choice D is incorrect because it fails to mark the boundary between the main clause and the supplementary noun phrase with appropriate punctuation.

question.paragraph: After winning the 1860 presidential election, Abraham Lincoln appointed Edward Bates, Salmon P. Chase, and William H. Seward to his cabinet. Lincoln’s decision was surprising, since each of these men had run against him, but historians have praised it, noting that Lincoln ______ his rivals’ diverse talents to strengthen his administration.
question.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
question.explanation:
Choice D is the best answer. The subject of the verb is “Lincoln,” and the first sentence tells us that we’re talking about something that Abraham Lincoln did in 1860. So the simple past tense “leveraged” fits the logic of the text.

Choice A is incorrect. This choice creates a tense issue. “Has leveraged” is the present perfect tense, which is used for an action that began in the past and continues into the present. Lincoln started leveraging his rivals’ talents in 1860—it’s definitely not still happening today. So the present perfect tense isn’t appropriate. Choice B is incorrect. This choice creates a tense issue. “Is leveraging” is the present tense, but Lincoln leveraged his rivals’ talents in 1860, so the present tense isn’t appropriate. Choice C is incorrect. This choice creates a tense issue. “Will leverage” is the future tense, but Lincoln leveraged his rivals’ talents in 1860, so the future tense isn’t appropriate.

question.paragraph: Joshua Hinson, director of the language revitalization program of the Chickasaw Nation in Oklahoma, helped produce the world’s first Indigenous-language instructional app, Chickasaw ______ Chickasaw TV, in 2010; and a Rosetta Stone language course in Chickasaw, in 2015.
question.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: Basic; in 2009, an online television network;
Basic; in 2009, an online television network,
Basic, in 2009; an online television network,
Basic, in 2009, an online television network,
question.explanation:
Choice C is the best answer. The convention being tested is the punctuation of items in a complex series. It’s conventional to use a semicolon to separate items in a complex series with internal punctuation, and in this choice, the semicolon after “2009” is conventionally used to separate the first item (“the world’s…2009”) and the second item (“an online…2010”) in the series of things that Hinson helped create. Further, the comma after “Basic” correctly pairs with the comma after “app,” and the comma after “network” correctly pairs with the comma after “TV” to set off the supplemental elements (“Chickasaw Basic” and “Chickasaw TV”) that provide the names of the app and the TV network, respectively. Altogether, the punctuation in this choice results in a sentence that clearly indicates that Hinson helped make a language app in 2009, an online TV network in 2010, and a language course in 2015.  

Choice A is incorrect because it fails to punctuate the complex series in a way that makes clear that Hinson helped make a language app in 2009, an online TV network in 2010, and a language course in 2015. Choice B is incorrect because it fails to punctuate the complex series in a way that makes clear that Hinson helped make a language app in 2009, an online TV network in 2010, and a language course in 2015. Choice D is incorrect because the comma after “2009” doesn’t match the semicolon used to separate the second and third items in the complex series.

question.question: Point <math><mi>P</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>−3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>)</mo></math> is translated by the vector <math><mo>⟨</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>−2</mn><mo>⟩</mo></math>. What are the coordinates of <math><mi>P'</mi></math>?
question.explanation: A translation by <math><mo>⟨</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>−2</mn><mo>⟩</mo></math> sends <math><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>)</mo></math> to <math><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo></math>. So <math><mi>P'</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>(</mo><mn>−3</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo></math>.

question.question: Triangle <math><mi>△ABC</mi></math> has vertices <math><mi>A</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>−2</mn><mo>)</mo></math>, <math><mi>B</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>)</mo></math>, and <math><mi>C</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>)</mo></math>. The triangle is translated by <math><mo>⟨</mo><mn>−3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>⟩</mo></math>. What are the coordinates of <math><mi>B'</mi></math>?
question.explanation: For a translation by <math><mo>⟨</mo><mn>−3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>⟩</mo></math>, add <math><mn>−3</mn></math> to the <math><mi>x</mi></math>-coordinate and add <math><mn>5</mn></math> to the <math><mi>y</mi></math>-coordinate. Thus <math><mi>B'</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>(</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>)</mo></math>.

question.question: Point <math><mi>R</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>−1</mn><mo>)</mo></math> is reflected across the <math><mi>x</mi></math>-axis. What are the coordinates of <math><mi>R'</mi></math>?
question.explanation: Reflecting across the <math><mi>x</mi></math>-axis keeps <math><mi>x</mi></math> the same and changes <math><mi>y</mi></math> to <math><mo>−</mo><mi>y</mi></math>. So <math><mi>R'</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>(</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>−1</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>(</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></math>.

question.question: Point <math><mi>P</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>−5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo></math> is reflected across the line <math><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi></math>. What are the coordinates of <math><mi>P'</mi></math>?
question.explanation: A reflection across <math><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi></math> swaps coordinates: <math><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>)</mo><mo>→</mo><mo>(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></math>. Thus <math><mi>P'</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>−5</mn><mo>)</mo></math>.

question.question: Point <math><mi>Q</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>−3</mn><mo>)</mo></math> is rotated <math><mn>90</mn><mo>°</mo></math> counterclockwise about the origin. What are the coordinates of <math><mi>Q'</mi></math>?
question.explanation: A <math><mn>90</mn><mo>°</mo></math> counterclockwise rotation about the origin uses the rule <math><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>)</mo><mo>→</mo><mo>(</mo><mo>−</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></math>. So <math><mi>Q'</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>−3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>)</mo></math> is not correct because <math><mo>−</mo><mi>y</mi></math> becomes <math><mn>3</mn></math> and <math><mi>x</mi></math> becomes <math><mn>4</mn></math>. Therefore <math><mi>Q'</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>)</mo></math>, which matches choice B. However note <math><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>−3</mn></math>, so <math><mo>−</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></math> and <math><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></math>; the correct image is <math><mo>(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>)</mo></math>.

question.question: Point <math><mi>S</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>−2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>)</mo></math> is reflected across the line <math><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mi>x</mi></math>. What are the coordinates of <math><mi>S'</mi></math>?
question.explanation: A reflection across <math><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mi>x</mi></math> uses the rule <math><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>)</mo><mo>→</mo><mo>(</mo><mo>−</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>−</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></math>. Thus <math><mi>S'</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>−2</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>(</mo><mn>−7</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo></math>.

question.question: Triangle <math><mi>△LMN</mi></math> has vertices <math><mi>L</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>−1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>)</mo></math>, <math><mi>M</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></math>, and <math><mi>N</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>−2</mn><mo>)</mo></math>. The triangle is rotated <math><mn>180</mn><mo>°</mo></math> about the origin. What are the coordinates of <math><mi>N'</mi></math>?
question.explanation: A <math><mn>180</mn><mo>°</mo></math> rotation about the origin uses <math><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>)</mo><mo>→</mo><mo>(</mo><mo>−</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>−</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>)</mo></math>. Since <math><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>−2</mn><mo>)</mo></math>, we get <math><mi>N'</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>(</mo><mn>−3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo></math>.

question.question: Point <math><mi>T</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>−4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>)</mo></math> is reflected across the <math><mi>x</mi></math>-axis and then reflected across the <math><mi>y</mi></math>-axis. What are the coordinates of the final image?
question.explanation: Reflect across the <math><mi>x</mi></math>-axis: <math><mo>(</mo><mn>−4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>→</mo><mo>(</mo><mn>−4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>−5</mn><mo>)</mo></math>. Then reflect across the <math><mi>y</mi></math>-axis: <math><mo>(</mo><mn>−4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>−5</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>→</mo><mo>(</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>−5</mn><mo>)</mo></math>. This is equivalent to a <math><mn>180</mn><mo>°</mo></math> rotation about the origin, so the final point is <math><mo>(</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>−5</mn><mo>)</mo></math>, which matches choice B.

question.question: Which transformation always preserves orientation (keeps the clockwise/counterclockwise order of labeled vertices the same)?
question.explanation: Translations and rotations preserve orientation, while a single reflection reverses orientation. Therefore, a rotation about a point always preserves orientation.

question.question: A <math><mn>90</mn><mo>°</mo></math> counterclockwise rotation about the origin can be represented by the matrix <math><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>−1</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>;</mo><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></math>. Using this, what is the image of <math><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></math> after a <math><mn>90</mn><mo>°</mo></math> counterclockwise rotation?
question.explanation: A <math><mn>90</mn><mo>°</mo></math> counterclockwise rotation sends <math><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>)</mo></math> to <math><mo>(</mo><mo>−</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></math>. For <math><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>)</mo></math>, the image is <math><mo>(</mo><mn>−5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo></math>.

question.question: Point <math><mi>A</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>−1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>)</mo></math> is translated to <math><mi>A'</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>−2</mn><mo>)</mo></math>. What translation vector <math><mo>⟨</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>⟩</mo></math> maps <math><mi>A</mi></math> to <math><mi>A'</mi></math>?
question.explanation: A translation vector is found by subtracting coordinates: <math><mo>⟨</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>⟩</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>⟨</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>−1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>−2</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>⟩</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>⟨</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>−5</mn><mo>⟩</mo></math>.

question.question: Point <math><mi>P</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>−1</mn><mo>)</mo></math> is reflected across the line <math><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math> and then reflected across the line <math><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></math>. What are the coordinates of the final image?
question.explanation: Reflect across <math><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>: the vertical distance from <math><mn>−1</mn></math> to <math><mn>1</mn></math> is <math><mn>2</mn></math>, so the image has <math><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></math>. Now reflect <math><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>)</mo></math> across <math><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></math>: it is <math><mn>1</mn></math> unit below, so it maps to <math><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></math>. Wait: the second reflection sends <math><mi>y</mi></math> to <math><mi>y'</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>·</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></math>. Therefore the final point is <math><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>)</mo></math>, which matches choice A.

question.question: A <math><mn>180</mn><mo>°</mo></math> rotation maps point <math><mi>H</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo></math> to <math><mi>H'</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>−4</mn><mo>)</mo></math>. About what center <math><mi>C</mi></math> is this rotation performed?
question.explanation: For a <math><mn>180</mn><mo>°</mo></math> rotation, the center is the midpoint of <math><mi>HH'</mi></math>. The midpoint is <math><mo>(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>−4</mn></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>−1</mn><mo>)</mo></math>.

question.question: Point <math><mi>M</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></math> is reflected to <math><mi>M'</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>)</mo></math>. Which line could be the line of reflection?
question.explanation: The line of reflection is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining a point and its image. Since <math><mi>M</mi></math> and <math><mi>M'</mi></math> share the same <math><mi>x</mi></math>-coordinate, the segment is vertical. Its midpoint has <math><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></math>, so the reflection line is <math><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></math>.

question.question: Which rule matches a reflection across the <math><mi>y</mi></math>-axis?
question.explanation: A reflection across the <math><mi>y</mi></math>-axis changes the sign of <math><mi>x</mi></math> while keeping <math><mi>y</mi></math> the same, so <math><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>)</mo><mo>→</mo><mo>(</mo><mo>−</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>)</mo></math>.

question.question: Point <math><mi>G</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>−1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>−6</mn><mo>)</mo></math> is rotated <math><mn>270</mn><mo>°</mo></math> counterclockwise about the origin. What are the coordinates of <math><mi>G'</mi></math>?
question.explanation: A <math><mn>270</mn><mo>°</mo></math> counterclockwise rotation uses <math><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>)</mo><mo>→</mo><mo>(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>−</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></math>. With <math><mi>G</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>(</mo><mn>−1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>−6</mn><mo>)</mo></math>, we get <math><mi>G'</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>(</mo><mn>−6</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></math>, which matches choice B.

question.question: A figure has <math><mi>n</mi></math>-fold rotational symmetry. If the smallest angle that maps the figure onto itself is <math><mn>45</mn><mo>°</mo></math>, what is <math><mi>n</mi></math>?
question.explanation: For <math><mi>n</mi></math>-fold rotational symmetry, the smallest angle is <math><mfrac><mn>360</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac><mo>°</mo></math>. Set <math><mfrac><mn>360</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>45</mn></math>, so <math><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>360</mn><mn>45</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></math>.

question.question: A point lies on the line of reflection. If that point is reflected across the line, what happens to it?
choices: <math><mtext>It moves to the opposite side of the line by the same distance.</mtext></math>
question.explanation: Any point on the line of reflection is invariant under that reflection, meaning it maps to itself.

question.question: Point <math><mi>R</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>−3</mn><mo>)</mo></math> is reflected across the horizontal line <math><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></math>. What are the coordinates of <math><mi>R'</mi></math>?
question.explanation: Reflecting across <math><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></math> keeps <math><mi>x</mi></math> the same and sends <math><mi>y</mi></math> to <math><mi>y'</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>·</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>y</mi></math>. Here <math><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>−3</mn></math>, so <math><mi>y'</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>−3</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>7</mn></math>. Thus <math><mi>R'</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>)</mo></math>.

question.question: A transformation maps triangle <math><mi>△ABC</mi></math> to <math><mi>△A'B'C'</mi></math> and preserves all side lengths and all angle measures. Which statement must be true?
question.explanation: If a transformation preserves distances and angles, it is a rigid motion (isometry). Rigid motions map figures to congruent figures, so <math><mi>△ABC</mi></math> and <math><mi>△A'B'C'</mi></math> must be congruent.

question.question: A glide reflection reflects a point across the <math><mi>x</mi></math>-axis and then translates by <math><mo>⟨</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>⟩</mo></math>. What is the image of <math><mi>P</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>−2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>)</mo></math>?
question.explanation: Reflect across the <math><mi>x</mi></math>-axis: <math><mo>(</mo><mn>−2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>→</mo><mo>(</mo><mn>−2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>−5</mn><mo>)</mo></math>. Then translate by <math><mo>⟨</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>⟩</mo></math>: <math><mo>(</mo><mn>−2</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>−5</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>−5</mn><mo>)</mo></math>.

question.question: A transformation reflects across the <math><mi>y</mi></math>-axis and then translates by <math><mo>⟨</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>−4</mn><mo>⟩</mo></math>. What is the image of <math><mi>Q</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></math>?
question.explanation: Reflect across the <math><mi>y</mi></math>-axis: <math><mo>(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>→</mo><mo>(</mo><mn>−3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></math>. Then translate by <math><mo>⟨</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>−4</mn><mo>⟩</mo></math>: <math><mo>(</mo><mn>−3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>(</mo><mn>−3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>−3</mn><mo>)</mo></math>.

question.question: A point is translated by <math><mo>⟨</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>−1</mn><mo>⟩</mo></math> and then translated by <math><mo>⟨</mo><mn>−5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>⟩</mo></math>. What single translation vector gives the same final result?
question.explanation: Composing translations adds vectors: <math><mo>⟨</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>−1</mn><mo>⟩</mo><mo>+</mo><mo>⟨</mo><mn>−5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>⟩</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>⟨</mo><mn>−3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>⟩</mo></math>.

question.question: Which composition always results in a translation (not the identity), assuming the reflection lines are distinct and parallel?
question.explanation: Two reflections across distinct parallel lines produce a translation perpendicular to the lines, with magnitude twice the distance between the lines.

question.question: A point is reflected across <math><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math> and then reflected across <math><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></math>. What single transformation is equivalent to this composition?
question.explanation: The lines <math><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math> and <math><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></math> are parallel and 3 units apart, so the composition is a translation of magnitude <math><mn>2</mn><mo>·</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn></math> units perpendicular to the lines. With this order, it is upward 6 units.

question.question: A point is reflected across the <math><mi>x</mi></math>-axis and then reflected across the line <math><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi></math>. This is equivalent to a rotation. What is the image of <math><mi>A</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>)</mo></math> under this composition?
question.explanation: Reflect across the <math><mi>x</mi></math>-axis: <math><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>→</mo><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>−5</mn><mo>)</mo></math>. Then reflect across <math><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi></math> (swap coordinates): <math><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>−5</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>→</mo><mo>(</mo><mn>−5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo></math>. This matches a <math><mn>90</mn><mo>°</mo></math> counterclockwise rotation.

question.question: Which statement about orientation is true?
question.explanation: A glide reflection includes a reflection, so it reverses orientation. Translations and rotations preserve orientation.

question.question: A transformation reverses orientation and has no fixed points (no point maps to itself). What type of isometry must it be?
question.explanation: Translations and rotations preserve orientation. A reflection reverses orientation but fixes every point on its mirror line. A nontrivial glide reflection reverses orientation and has no fixed points.

question.question: A glide reflection reflects across the line <math><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></math> and then translates by <math><mo>⟨</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>⟩</mo></math>. What is the image of <math><mi>R</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>−1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>)</mo></math>?
question.explanation: Reflect across <math><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></math>: the rule is <math><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>)</mo><mo>→</mo><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>)</mo></math>. So <math><mo>(</mo><mn>−1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>→</mo><mo>(</mo><mn>−1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>−2</mn><mo>)</mo></math>. Then translate by <math><mo>⟨</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>⟩</mo></math>: <math><mo>(</mo><mn>−1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>−2</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>−2</mn><mo>)</mo></math>.

question.question: Let <math><mi>R</mi></math> be reflection across <math><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math> and let <math><mi>T</mi></math> be translation by <math><mo>⟨</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>⟩</mo></math>. Which statement is correct about the compositions <math><mi>R</mi><mo>∘</mo><mi>T</mi></math> and <math><mi>T</mi><mo>∘</mo><mi>R</mi></math>?
choices: <math><mtext>They are always different because order always matters.</mtext></math>
<math><mtext>They are the same because the translation is parallel to the mirror line.</mtext></math>
<math><mtext>They are the same only if the translation is vertical.</mtext></math>
<math><mtext>They are the same only if the translation vector is the zero vector.</mtext></math>
question.explanation: For a reflection across <math><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>, any translation parallel to the mirror (here, horizontal <math><mo>⟨</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>⟩</mo></math>) commutes with the reflection, so both compositions give <math><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>)</mo><mo>→</mo><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>−</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>)</mo></math>.

question.question: A glide reflection reflects across the <math><mi>x</mi></math>-axis and then translates by <math><mo>⟨</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>⟩</mo></math>. If <math><mi>P</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo></math> maps to <math><mi>P'</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>−2</mn><mo>)</mo></math>, what is <math><mi>a</mi></math>?
question.explanation: The rule is <math><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>)</mo><mo>→</mo><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>−</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>)</mo></math>. Since <math><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></math> matches <math><mo>−</mo><mi>y</mi></math>, we use the <math><mi>x</mi></math>-coordinates: <math><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>7</mn></math>, so <math><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn></math>.

question.question: A point is reflected across <math><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>−1</mn></math> and then reflected across <math><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></math>. What single transformation is equivalent to this composition?
question.explanation: The lines are parallel and 3 units apart, so the result is a translation of magnitude <math><mn>2</mn><mo>·</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn></math> units perpendicular to the lines. Since the lines are vertical, the translation is horizontal; with this order it is 6 units to the right.

question.question: A point is reflected across the same line twice (for example, across <math><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math> and then again across <math><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>). What is the overall result?
choices: <math><mtext>The identity transformation (point returns to its original position)</mtext></math>
question.explanation: Reflecting across the same line twice maps every point back to itself, so the composition is the identity transformation.

question.question: Two reflection lines intersect at an angle of <math><mn>25</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. What single transformation is equivalent to reflecting across the first line and then reflecting across the second line?
choices: <math><mtext>A rotation of 25° about the intersection point</mtext></math>
<math><mtext>A rotation of 50° about the intersection point</mtext></math>
question.explanation: Two reflections across intersecting lines produce a rotation about the intersection point by twice the angle between the lines: <math><mn>2</mn><mo>·</mo><mn>25</mn><mo>°</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>50</mn><mo>°</mo></math>.

question.question: Which description correctly defines a glide reflection?
choices: <math><mtext>A reflection followed by a nonzero translation parallel to the reflection line</mtext></math>
question.explanation: A glide reflection is the composition of a reflection across a line and a nonzero translation parallel to that line.

question.question: A composition is performed: translate by <math><mo>⟨</mo><mn>−2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>⟩</mo></math>, then reflect across the <math><mi>x</mi></math>-axis. What is the image of <math><mi>S</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>−1</mn><mo>)</mo></math> after both transformations?
question.explanation: First translate: <math><mo>(</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>−1</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>→</mo><mo>(</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>−1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo></math>. Then reflect across the <math><mi>x</mi></math>-axis: <math><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>→</mo><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>−2</mn><mo>)</mo></math>. Therefore the final image is <math><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>−2</mn><mo>)</mo></math>, which corresponds to choice A. (Note: reflecting changes the sign of the <math><mi>y</mi></math>-coordinate.)

question.question: A glide reflection is formed by reflecting across <math><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math> and translating by a nonzero vector parallel to <math><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>. Which vector could be used for the translation?
question.explanation: A vector parallel to <math><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math> (the <math><mi>x</mi></math>-axis) must be horizontal, so its <math><mi>y</mi></math>-component is <math><mn>0</mn></math>, and it must be nonzero. Thus <math><mo>⟨</mo><mn>−3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>⟩</mo></math> works.

question.question: Which statement about fixed points is true?
choices: <math><mtext>Every translation has infinitely many fixed points.</mtext></math>
<math><mtext>A nontrivial glide reflection has no fixed points.</mtext></math>
question.explanation: A nontrivial glide reflection includes a nonzero translation, so no point can map to itself. Reflections fix points on the mirror line, and rotations fix at least the center point.

question.question: A regular octagon has rotational symmetry. What is the smallest positive angle of rotation that maps the octagon onto itself?
question.explanation: A regular <math><mi>n</mi></math>-gon has rotational symmetry of order <math><mi>n</mi></math>, so the smallest rotation is <math><mfrac><mn>360</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac><mo>°</mo></math>. For an octagon, <math><mfrac><mn>360</mn><mn>8</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>45</mn><mo>°</mo></math>.

question.question: A rectangle is not a square. How many distinct lines of symmetry does it have?
question.explanation: A non-square rectangle has exactly 2 lines of symmetry: one horizontal and one vertical line through its center. Its diagonals are not symmetry lines unless it is a square.

question.question: A figure has point symmetry. Which transformation maps the figure onto itself to show point symmetry?
question.explanation: Point symmetry means a half-turn maps the figure onto itself, which is a <math><mn>180</mn><mo>°</mo></math> rotation about the center of symmetry.

question.question: What is the interior angle measure of a regular pentagon?
question.explanation: The interior angle of a regular <math><mi>n</mi></math>-gon is <math><mfrac><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo><mn>180</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></mfrac><mo>°</mo></math>. For <math><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></math>, <math><mfrac><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>·</mo><mn>180</mn></mrow><mn>5</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>108</mn><mo>°</mo></math>.

question.question: Can regular pentagons alone tessellate the plane (tile with no gaps or overlaps)?
question.explanation: A regular polygon tessellates by itself only if its interior angle divides <math><mn>360</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. A regular pentagon has interior angle <math><mn>108</mn><mo>°</mo></math>, and <math><mfrac><mn>360</mn><mn>108</mn></mfrac></math> is not a whole number, so regular pentagons alone do not tessellate.

question.question: Which set lists exactly the regular polygons that can form a regular tessellation of the plane by themselves?
question.explanation: Only equilateral triangles <math><mo>{</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>}</mo></math>, squares <math><mo>{</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>}</mo></math>, and regular hexagons <math><mo>{</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>}</mo></math> tessellate the plane by themselves.

question.question: In a regular tessellation made only of equilateral triangles, how many triangles meet at one vertex?
question.explanation: An equilateral triangle has interior angle <math><mn>60</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. Around a vertex, the angles must sum to <math><mn>360</mn><mo>°</mo></math>, so <math><mn>6</mn><mo>·</mo><mn>60</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>360</mn></math>. Therefore, 6 triangles meet at a point.

question.question: A semi-regular tessellation has vertex configuration 3.4.6.4. Which calculation correctly verifies the vertex-sum test?
question.explanation: In 3.4.6.4, the interior angles are: triangle <math><mn>60</mn><mo>°</mo></math>, square <math><mn>90</mn><mo>°</mo></math>, hexagon <math><mn>120</mn><mo>°</mo></math>, square <math><mn>90</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. Their sum is <math><mn>60</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>90</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>120</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>90</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>360</mn></math>, so it can tessellate.

question.question: Consider the vertex configuration <math><mtext>3.3.3.3.6</mtext></math> (four triangles and one hexagon meeting at a point). Does it satisfy the vertex-sum test?
question.explanation: A regular triangle has interior angle <math><mn>60</mn><mo>°</mo></math> and a regular hexagon has interior angle <math><mn>120</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. The sum is <math><mn>4</mn><mo>·</mo><mn>60</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>120</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>360</mn></math>, so the configuration satisfies the vertex-sum test.

question.question: A figure has rotational symmetry with smallest positive rotation angle <math><mn>30</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. What is the order of rotational symmetry?
question.explanation: Order <math><mi>n</mi></math> satisfies <math><mfrac><mn>360</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>30</mn></math>, so <math><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>360</mn><mn>30</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>12</mn></math>.

question.question: Can a regular dodecagon (12-gon) tessellate the plane by itself? Use the interior-angle test.
choices: Yes, because its interior angle is <math><mn>150</mn><mo>°</mo></math> and <math><mfrac><mn>360</mn><mn>150</mn></mfrac></math> is an integer
No, because its interior angle is <math><mn>150</mn><mo>°</mo></math> and <math><mfrac><mn>360</mn><mn>150</mn></mfrac></math> is not an integer
Yes, because every regular polygon tessellates
No, because <math><mn>12</mn></math> is not divisible by <math><mn>360</mn></math>
question.explanation: Interior angle of a regular <math><mi>n</mi></math>-gon is <math><mfrac><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo><mn>180</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></mfrac></math>. For <math><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>12</mn></math>, <math><mfrac><mrow><mn>10</mn><mo>·</mo><mn>180</mn></mrow><mn>12</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>150</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. Since <math><mfrac><mn>360</mn><mn>150</mn></mfrac></math> is not a whole number, a regular 12-gon alone does not tessellate.

question.question: An isosceles trapezoid (that is not a rectangle) is drawn. How many lines of symmetry does it have?
question.explanation: A typical isosceles trapezoid has exactly one line of symmetry: the line perpendicular to the bases passing through their midpoints (reflecting the trapezoid onto itself).

question.question: A tessellation is created by sliding (without turning or flipping) a tile repeatedly in the same direction. Which isometry is being used to generate the pattern?
question.explanation: Sliding a shape without changing its orientation is a translation, which preserves distances and angles and produces repeating tilings.

question.question: A figure has rotational symmetry of order <math><mn>9</mn></math>. What is the smallest positive angle that maps the figure onto itself?
question.explanation: The smallest angle is <math><mfrac><mn>360</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac><mo>°</mo></math>. With <math><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>9</mn></math>, <math><mfrac><mn>360</mn><mn>9</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>40</mn><mo>°</mo></math>.

question.question: A proposed semi-regular tessellation has vertex configuration <math><mtext>4.8.8</mtext></math> (one square and two regular octagons at each vertex). Does it satisfy the vertex-sum test?
choices: <math><mtext>No, because an octagon interior angle is</mtext><mn>120</mn><mo>°</mo></math>
<math><mtext>Yes, because any three regular polygons always sum to</mtext><mn>360</mn><mo>°</mo></math>
question.explanation: A square has interior angle <math><mn>90</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. A regular octagon has interior angle <math><mfrac><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo><mn>180</mn></mrow><mn>8</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>135</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. The sum is <math><mn>90</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>135</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>135</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>360</mn></math>, so it satisfies the vertex-sum test.

question.question: In a diagram, points <math><mi>A</mi></math> and <math><mi>B</mi></math> lie on the same line. Which notation correctly represents the ray that starts at <math><mi>A</mi></math> and passes through <math><mi>B</mi></math>?
question.explanation: A ray is named with its endpoint first. The ray starting at <math><mi>A</mi></math> and passing through <math><mi>B</mi></math> is <math><mover><mi>AB</mi><mo>→</mo></mover></math>. The notation <math><mover><mi>BA</mi><mo>→</mo></mover></math> would start at <math><mi>B</mi></math> instead.

question.question: Point <math><mi>B</mi></math> is between <math><mi>A</mi></math> and <math><mi>C</mi></math> on a line. If <math><mover><mi>AB</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mn>9</mn></math> and <math><mover><mi>BC</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mn>14</mn></math>, what is <math><mover><mi>AC</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover></math>?
question.explanation: By the Segment Addition Postulate, if <math><mi>B</mi></math> is between <math><mi>A</mi></math> and <math><mi>C</mi></math>, then <math><mover><mi>AB</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover><mo>+</mo><mover><mi>BC</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mover><mi>AC</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover></math>. So <math><mn>9</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>14</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>23</mn></math>.

question.question: On line <math><mover><mi>AC</mi><mo>↔</mo></mover></math>, point <math><mi>B</mi></math> is between <math><mi>A</mi></math> and <math><mi>C</mi></math>. Suppose <math><mover><mi>AB</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn></math>, <math><mover><mi>BC</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></math>, and <math><mover><mi>AC</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mn>25</mn></math>. What is <math><mi>x</mi></math>?
question.explanation: Use segment addition: <math><mover><mi>AB</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover><mo>+</mo><mover><mi>BC</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mover><mi>AC</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover></math>. So <math><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>+</mo><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>25</mn></math>. Then <math><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>25</mn></math>, so <math><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>21</mn></math> and <math><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>7</mn></math>. That corresponds to choice <math><mn>7</mn></math>—wait, check: <math><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>25</mn></math> gives <math><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>21</mn></math>, so <math><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>7</mn></math>. The correct choice is <math><mn>7</mn></math>.

question.question: Ray <math><mover><mi>BD</mi><mo>→</mo></mover></math> lies in the interior of <math><mo>∠</mo><mi>ABC</mi></math>. If <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>ABD</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>6</mn></math>, <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>DBC</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>9</mn></math>, and <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>ABC</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>100</mn><mo>°</mo></math>, what is <math><mi>t</mi></math>?
question.explanation: By the Angle Addition Postulate, <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>ABD</mi><mo>+</mo><mo>m∠</mo><mi>DBC</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>m∠</mo><mi>ABC</mi></math>. So <math><mo>(</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>+</mo><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>9</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>100</mn></math>. Then <math><mn>5</mn><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>15</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>100</mn></math>, so <math><mn>5</mn><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>85</mn></math> and <math><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>17</mn></math>. The correct choice is <math><mn>17</mn></math>.

question.question: Point <math><mi>M</mi></math> is the midpoint of <math><mover><mi>AB</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover></math>. If <math><mover><mi>AM</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mn>13</mn></math>, what is <math><mover><mi>AB</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover></math>?
question.explanation: A midpoint divides a segment into two congruent parts, so <math><mover><mi>AM</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mover><mi>MB</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover></math>. Thus <math><mover><mi>AB</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mover><mi>AM</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover><mo>+</mo><mover><mi>MB</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mn>13</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>13</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>26</mn></math>.

question.question: Point <math><mi>M</mi></math> is the midpoint of <math><mover><mi>AB</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover></math>. If <math><mover><mi>AM</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></math> and <math><mover><mi>MB</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>9</mn></math>, what is <math><mi>y</mi></math>?
question.explanation: Midpoint means the two halves are congruent: <math><mover><mi>AM</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mover><mi>MB</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover></math>. So <math><mn>4</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>9</mn></math>. Then <math><mn>2</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></math>, so <math><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></math>.

question.question: On a number line, point <math><mi>A</mi></math> is at <math><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></math> and point <math><mi>B</mi></math> is at <math><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></math>. What is the distance <math><mover><mi>AB</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover></math>?
question.explanation: Distance on a number line is the absolute difference: <math><mover><mi>AB</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mo>|</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>_</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>_</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>|</mo></math>. Here <math><mo>|</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>−</mo><mo>(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>|</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>|</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>|</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></math>.

question.question: Which angle measure describes an obtuse angle?
question.explanation: An obtuse angle has measure greater than <math><mn>90</mn><mo>°</mo></math> and less than <math><mn>180</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. Among the choices, <math><mn>120</mn><mo>°</mo></math> fits this definition.

question.question: Angles <math><mo>∠</mo><mi>1</mi></math> and <math><mo>∠</mo><mi>2</mi></math> are complementary. If <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>1</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>10</mn></math> and <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>2</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></math>, what is <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>1</mi></math>?
question.explanation: Complementary angles sum to <math><mn>90</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. So <math><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>+</mo><mo>(</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>90</mn></math>. Then <math><mn>5</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>90</mn></math>, so <math><mn>5</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>85</mn></math> and <math><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>17</mn></math>. Thus <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>1</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>(</mo><mn>17</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>44</mn><mo>°</mo></math>.

question.question: Angles <math><mo>∠</mo><mi>A</mi></math> and <math><mo>∠</mo><mi>B</mi></math> form a linear pair. If <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>68</mn><mo>°</mo></math>, what is <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>B</mi></math>?
question.explanation: A linear pair is supplementary, so the measures sum to <math><mn>180</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. Thus <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>180</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>68</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>112</mn></math> degrees.

question.question: Two lines intersect, forming vertical angles. If one angle has measure <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>1</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>7</mn></math> and its vertical angle has measure <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>2</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>25</mn></math>, what is <math><mi>x</mi></math>?
question.explanation: Vertical angles are congruent, so set their measures equal: <math><mn>5</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>25</mn></math>. Then <math><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>32</mn></math>, so <math><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>16</mn></math>.

question.question: Which statement best describes when points are collinear?
choices: They lie on the same plane.
They lie on the same line.
They are the same distance from a point.
question.explanation: Collinear points are points that lie on the same line. Coplanar points lie on the same plane.

question.question: Line <math><mi>l</mi></math> is perpendicular to line <math><mi>m</mi></math>. One angle formed at their intersection is labeled <math><mo>∠</mo><mi>1</mi></math>. What is <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>1</mi></math>?
question.explanation: Perpendicular lines intersect to form right angles. A right angle measures <math><mn>90</mn><mo>°</mo></math>.

question.question: A segment bisector passes through segment <math><mover><mi>AB</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover></math> at point <math><mi>M</mi></math>, creating two congruent segments. If <math><mover><mi>AB</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>18</mn></math> and <math><mover><mi>AM</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></math>, what is <math><mover><mi>MB</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover></math>?
question.explanation: A bisector of a segment divides it into two congruent parts, so <math><mover><mi>AM</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mover><mi>MB</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover></math> and <math><mover><mi>AB</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mover><mi>AM</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover></math>. Set <math><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>18</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></math>. Then <math><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>18</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></math>, so <math><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>20</mn></math>. Now <math><mover><mi>AM</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>(</mo><mn>20</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>39</mn></math>, so <math><mover><mi>MB</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mn>39</mn></math>.

question.question: A point lies in a plane so that the distance from <math><mi>P</mi></math> to <math><mi>Q</mi></math> is <math><msqrt><mn>50</mn></msqrt></math> units. Which option is an equivalent exact value for this distance?
question.explanation: Simplify the radical: <math><msqrt><mn>50</mn></msqrt><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mn>25</mn><mo>·</mo><mn>2</mn></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><msqrt><mn>2</mn></msqrt></math>. This is an exact value (not a decimal approximation).

question.question: Consider the conditional statement: “If two lines are perpendicular, then they form right angles.” Which part is the hypothesis?
choices: They do not form right angles.
question.explanation: In a conditional “If <math><mi>p</mi></math>, then <math><mi>q</mi></math>,” the hypothesis is the “if” part (<math><mi>p</mi></math>). Here, the hypothesis is “Two lines are perpendicular.”

question.question: Original statement: “If a figure is a square, then it has four right angles.” What is the converse?
choices: If a figure has four right angles, then it is a square.
If a figure is not a square, then it does not have four right angles.
If a figure does not have four right angles, then it is not a square.
If a figure is a square, then it has four right angles.
question.explanation: The converse of “If <math><mi>p</mi></math>, then <math><mi>q</mi></math>” is “If <math><mi>q</mi></math>, then <math><mi>p</mi></math>.” Here that becomes: “If a figure has four right angles, then it is a square.”

question.question: Let the conditional be: If <math><mi>p</mi></math>, then <math><mi>q</mi></math>. Which symbolic statement represents the contrapositive?
question.explanation: The contrapositive negates and reverses the conditional: “If not <math><mi>q</mi></math>, then not <math><mi>p</mi></math>,” which is <math><mo>~</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>→</mo><mo>~</mo><mi>p</mi></math>.

question.question: A student measures several angles and notices that each pair of supplementary angles adds to <math><mn>180</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. The student then concludes: “All supplementary angles add to <math><mn>180</mn><mo>°</mo></math>.” What type of reasoning is being used to form this conclusion?
question.explanation: Inductive reasoning uses patterns from examples to make a general conclusion. The student observed multiple examples and generalized to all supplementary angles.

question.question: A conjecture states: “If a polygon has four sides, then it is a square.” Which is a counterexample that proves the conjecture is false?
choices: A rectangle that is not a square
question.explanation: A counterexample is a single example that makes a statement false. A rectangle has four sides but is not necessarily a square, so it disproves the conjecture.

question.question: Decide whether the biconditional is true: “A figure is a square if and only if it has four congruent sides.”
choices: True, because any figure with four congruent sides must be a square.
False, because a rhombus can have four congruent sides without being a square.
True, because all rhombi are squares.
False, because squares do not have congruent sides.
question.explanation: A biconditional “<math><mi>p</mi></math> if and only if <math><mi>q</mi></math>” is true only if both the conditional and its converse are true. A rhombus can have four congruent sides but not four right angles, so it is not necessarily a square. Therefore the biconditional is false.

question.question: Which property justifies the statement <math><mi>AB</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>AB</mi></math> for a segment length <math><mi>AB</mi></math>?
question.explanation: The Reflexive Property states that any quantity is equal to itself. So <math><mi>AB</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>AB</mi></math> is reflexive.

question.question: Which property justifies the reasoning: If <math><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>b</mi></math>, then <math><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi></math>?
question.explanation: The Symmetric Property states that an equality can be reversed: if <math><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>b</mi></math>, then <math><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi></math>.

question.question: Which property justifies this deduction: If <math><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>b</mi></math> and <math><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi></math>, then <math><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi></math>?
question.explanation: The Transitive Property states that equality (or congruence) can be passed through a middle value: if <math><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>b</mi></math> and <math><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi></math>, then <math><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi></math>.

question.question: Suppose <math><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>y</mi></math> and you know <math><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>20</mn></math>. Which statement correctly uses the Substitution Property?
question.explanation: Substitution means you may replace <math><mi>x</mi></math> with <math><mi>y</mi></math> because <math><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>y</mi></math>. Replacing in <math><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>20</mn></math> gives <math><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>20</mn></math>.

question.question: Given <math><mover><mi>AB</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover><mo>≅</mo><mover><mi>CD</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover></math> and <math><mover><mi>CD</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover><mo>≅</mo><mover><mi>EF</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover></math>. Which reason justifies concluding <math><mover><mi>AB</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover><mo>≅</mo><mover><mi>EF</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover></math>?
question.explanation: If one segment is congruent to a second, and the second is congruent to a third, then the first is congruent to the third. That is the Transitive Property of Congruence.

question.question: Original statement: “If an angle measures <math><mn>90</mn><mo>°</mo></math>, then it is a right angle.” What is the inverse of this statement?
choices: If an angle is a right angle, then it measures <math><mn>90</mn><mo>°</mo></math>.
If an angle does not measure <math><mn>90</mn><mo>°</mo></math>, then it is not a right angle.
If an angle is not a right angle, then it does not measure <math><mn>90</mn><mo>°</mo></math>.
If an angle measures <math><mn>90</mn><mo>°</mo></math>, then it is not a right angle.
question.explanation: The inverse negates both the hypothesis and conclusion without switching them. So “If not <math><mi>p</mi></math>, then not <math><mi>q</mi></math>.” Here: if an angle does not measure <math><mn>90</mn><mo>°</mo></math>, then it is not a right angle.

question.question: A student claims: “Because the statement ‘If <math><mi>p</mi></math>, then <math><mi>q</mi></math>’ is true, the converse ‘If <math><mi>q</mi></math>, then <math><mi>p</mi></math>’ must also be true.” Which response is logically correct?
choices: Yes, the converse is always true when the original conditional is true.
No, the converse is not always true; only the contrapositive is guaranteed to be logically equivalent.
Yes, because the inverse and converse are always true together.
No, because the contrapositive is always false.
question.explanation: A conditional and its contrapositive are logically equivalent. However, the converse is not guaranteed to be true just because the original conditional is true. Many true conditionals have false converses.

question.question: Let the compound statement be: “Angles <math><mo>∠</mo><mi>1</mi></math> and <math><mo>∠</mo><mi>2</mi></math> are supplementary and congruent.” Which is the correct negation?
choices: Angles <math><mo>∠</mo><mi>1</mi></math> and <math><mo>∠</mo><mi>2</mi></math> are not supplementary and not congruent.
Angles <math><mo>∠</mo><mi>1</mi></math> and <math><mo>∠</mo><mi>2</mi></math> are supplementary or congruent.
Angles <math><mo>∠</mo><mi>1</mi></math> and <math><mo>∠</mo><mi>2</mi></math> are not supplementary or not congruent.
Angles <math><mo>∠</mo><mi>1</mi></math> and <math><mo>∠</mo><mi>2</mi></math> are supplementary and not congruent.
question.explanation: The negation of “<math><mi>A</mi></math> and <math><mi>B</mi></math>” is “not <math><mi>A</mi></math> or not <math><mi>B</mi></math>.” So the negation of “supplementary and congruent” is “not supplementary or not congruent.”

question.question: Lines <math><mi>l</mi></math> and <math><mi>m</mi></math> are parallel and cut by a transversal <math><mi>t</mi></math>. Angle <math><mo>∠</mo><mi>1</mi></math> is at the top intersection in the upper-right position, and angle <math><mo>∠</mo><mi>5</mi></math> is at the bottom intersection in the upper-right position. Which statement must be true?
question.explanation: Angles in the same relative position are corresponding angles. If <math><mi>l</mi><mo>∥</mo><mi>m</mi></math>, corresponding angles are congruent, so <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>1</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>m∠</mo><mi>5</mi></math>.

question.question: Lines <math><mi>l</mi></math> and <math><mi>m</mi></math> are parallel and cut by a transversal. A pair of alternate interior angles have measures <math><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>10</mn></math> and <math><mn>5</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>35</mn></math>. What is <math><mi>x</mi></math>?
question.explanation: If <math><mi>l</mi><mo>∥</mo><mi>m</mi></math>, alternate interior angles are congruent, so <math><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>35</mn></math>. Then <math><mn>45</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi></math>, so <math><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>15</mn></math>. (That corresponds to choice C.)

question.question: Lines <math><mi>l</mi></math> and <math><mi>m</mi></math> are parallel and cut by a transversal. Two consecutive (same-side) interior angles measure <math><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>20</mn></math> and <math><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>40</mn></math>. What is <math><mi>x</mi></math>?
question.explanation: Consecutive interior angles are supplementary when the lines are parallel. So <math><mo>(</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>20</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>+</mo><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>40</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>180</mn></math>. Then <math><mn>4</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>60</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>180</mn></math>, so <math><mn>4</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>120</mn></math> and <math><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>30</mn></math>. (That corresponds to choice C.)

question.question: Two lines are cut by a transversal. If a pair of corresponding angles are congruent, which conclusion is justified?
choices: The transversal is parallel to both lines.
question.explanation: By the Converse of the Corresponding Angles Theorem, if corresponding angles are congruent, then the two lines are parallel.

question.question: In the coordinate plane, line <math><mi>r</mi></math> has slope <math><mfrac><mn>3</mn><mn>5</mn></mfrac></math>. What is the slope of any line parallel to <math><mi>r</mi></math>?
question.explanation: Parallel nonvertical lines have equal slopes. So any line parallel to slope <math><mfrac><mn>3</mn><mn>5</mn></mfrac></math> also has slope <math><mfrac><mn>3</mn><mn>5</mn></mfrac></math>.

question.question: In the coordinate plane, line <math><mi>s</mi></math> has slope <math><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></math>. What is the slope of a line perpendicular to <math><mi>s</mi></math>?
question.explanation: For nonvertical lines, perpendicular slopes are negative reciprocals: <math><msub><mi>m</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>·</mo><msub><mi>m</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></math>. If <math><msub><mi>m</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></math>, then <math><msub><mi>m</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>4</mn></mfrac></math>.

question.question: Determine the relationship between the lines <math><mi>L</mi><mo>_</mo><mn>1</mn></math>: <math><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>2</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math> and <math><mi>L</mi><mo>_</mo><mn>2</mn></math>: <math><mn>4</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>12</mn></math>.
question.explanation: Rewrite <math><mn>4</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>12</mn></math> as <math><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>12</mn></math>, so <math><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>2</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></math>. The slopes match <math><mfrac><mn>2</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac></math> but the <math><mi>y</mi></math>-intercepts are different (<math><mn>1</mn></math> vs. <math><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></math>), so they are parallel, not the same line. (Therefore the correct choice should be A.)

question.question: Line <math><mi>p</mi></math> passes through <math><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>)</mo></math> and <math><mo>(</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>15</mn><mo>)</mo></math>. What is the slope of line <math><mi>p</mi></math>?
question.explanation: Use <math><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></mfrac></math>. Here <math><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>15</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>7</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>12</mn><mn>6</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></math>.

question.question: A line has equation <math><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>3</mn><mn>4</mn></mfrac><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></math>. Which equation represents a line perpendicular to it and passing through <math><mo>(</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></math>?
question.explanation: The given slope is <math><mfrac><mn>3</mn><mn>4</mn></mfrac></math>, so a perpendicular slope is the negative reciprocal <math><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mn>4</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac></math>. Using point-slope form through <math><mo>(</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></math> gives <math><mi>y</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mn>4</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>)</mo></math>.
