question.question: Line <math><mi>M</mi></math> has equation <math><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn></math>. Which equation is parallel to <math><mi>M</mi></math> and passes through <math><mo>(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>)</mo></math>?
question.explanation: Rewrite <math><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn></math> as <math><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>2</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></math>, so the slope is <math><mfrac><mn>2</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac></math>. A parallel line must have the same slope, and passing through <math><mo>(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>)</mo></math> gives <math><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>2</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn></math>.

question.question: Lines <math><mi>l</mi></math> and <math><mi>m</mi></math> are parallel. A transversal <math><mi>t</mi></math> is perpendicular to <math><mi>l</mi></math>. What can you conclude about <math><mi>t</mi></math> and <math><mi>m</mi></math>?
question.explanation: By the Perpendicular Transversal Theorem, if a transversal is perpendicular to one of two parallel lines, then it is perpendicular to the other as well. So <math><mi>t</mi><mo>⟂</mo><mi>m</mi></math>.

question.question: Two lines are cut by a transversal. One pair of alternate exterior angles has measures <math><mn>7</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>10</mn></math> and <math><mn>4</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>26</mn></math>. If these two angles are congruent, what conclusion can you make about the two lines?
choices: The lines must intersect at a right angle.
No conclusion can be made without a diagram.
question.explanation: If a pair of alternate exterior angles are congruent, then by the Converse of the Alternate Exterior Angles Theorem, the lines are parallel. (You can also solve <math><mn>7</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>26</mn></math> to confirm consistency.)

question.question: Line <math><mi>a</mi></math> passes through <math><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>)</mo></math> and <math><mo>(</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></math>. Line <math><mi>b</mi></math> passes through <math><mo>(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>)</mo></math> and <math><mo>(</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>)</mo></math>. Are lines <math><mi>a</mi></math> and <math><mi>b</mi></math> perpendicular?
choices: Yes, because their slopes multiply to <math><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></math>.
Yes, because their slopes are equal.
No, because their slopes multiply to <math><mn>1</mn></math>.
No, because at least one line is vertical.
question.explanation: Slope of <math><mi>a</mi></math>: <math><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>6</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn><mn>4</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></math>. Slope of <math><mi>b</mi></math>: <math><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>7</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>4</mn><mn>8</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></math>. Product: <math><mo>(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>(</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></math>, not <math><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></math>, so they are not perpendicular. Therefore the correct choice should be not-perpendicular. (Choice A is incorrect; the correct choice is none of the above.)

question.question: Two lines intersect, forming angles. Which statement is always true, even if the lines are not parallel?
question.explanation: Vertical angles are formed by two intersecting lines and are always congruent. The other relationships depend on having parallel lines cut by a transversal.

question.question: Lines <math><mi>l</mi></math> and <math><mi>m</mi></math> are cut by transversal <math><mi>t</mi></math>. If a pair of consecutive interior angles measure <math><mn>112</mn><mo>°</mo></math> and <math><mn>68</mn><mo>°</mo></math>, what conclusion is justified?
question.explanation: Consecutive interior angles are supplementary if and only if the lines are parallel (converse). Since <math><mn>112</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>68</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>180</mn></math>, the angles are supplementary, so <math><mi>l</mi><mo>∥</mo><mi>m</mi></math>.

question.question: Two lines intersect, forming vertical angles. If one pair of vertical angles has measures <math><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>12</mn></math> and <math><mn>5</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>24</mn></math>, what is <math><mi>x</mi></math>?
question.explanation: Vertical angles are congruent, so set them equal: <math><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>12</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>24</mn></math>. Then <math><mn>36</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi></math>, so <math><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>18</mn></math>.

question.question: Angles <math><mo>∠</mo><mi>1</mi></math> and <math><mo>∠</mo><mi>2</mi></math> form a linear pair. If <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>1</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>68</mn><mo>°</mo></math>, what is <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>2</mi></math>?
question.explanation: A linear pair is supplementary, so the measures add to <math><mn>180</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. Thus <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>2</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>180</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>68</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>112</mn><mo>°</mo></math>.

question.question: Angles <math><mo>∠</mo><mi>A</mi></math> and <math><mo>∠</mo><mi>B</mi></math> are complementary. If <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>10</mn></math> and <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></math>, what is <math><mi>t</mi></math>?
question.explanation: Complementary angles sum to <math><mn>90</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. So <math><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>+</mo><mo>(</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>90</mn></math>. Then <math><mn>5</mn><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>90</mn></math>, so <math><mn>5</mn><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>85</mn></math> and <math><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>17</mn></math>.

question.question: Angles <math><mo>∠</mo><mi>P</mi></math> and <math><mo>∠</mo><mi>Q</mi></math> are supplementary. If <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>8</mn></math> and <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>Q</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>22</mn></math>, what is <math><mi>x</mi></math>?
question.explanation: Supplementary angles sum to <math><mn>180</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. So <math><mo>(</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>+</mo><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>22</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>180</mn></math>. Then <math><mn>6</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>30</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>180</mn></math>, so <math><mn>6</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>150</mn></math> and <math><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>25</mn></math>. (That corresponds to choice C.)

question.question: Point <math><mi>D</mi></math> lies in the interior of <math><mo>∠</mo><mi>ABC</mi></math>. If <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>ABD</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>35</mn><mo>°</mo></math> and <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>ABC</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>120</mn><mo>°</mo></math>, what is <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>DBC</mi></math>?
question.explanation: By the Angle Addition Postulate, <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>ABD</mi><mo>+</mo><mo>m∠</mo><mi>DBC</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>m∠</mo><mi>ABC</mi></math>. So <math><mn>35</mn><mo>+</mo><mo>m∠</mo><mi>DBC</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>120</mn></math>, giving <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>DBC</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>85</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. (That corresponds to choice C.)

question.question: Ray <math><mover><mi>BD</mi><mo>→</mo></mover></math> bisects <math><mo>∠</mo><mi>ABC</mi></math>. If <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>ABD</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>7</mn></math> and <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>DBC</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></math>, what is <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>ABC</mi></math>?
question.explanation: An angle bisector makes two congruent angles, so <math><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></math>. Then <math><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></math>. Each half is <math><mn>2</mn><mo>(</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>27</mn><mo>°</mo></math>, so the whole angle is <math><mn>27</mn><mo>°</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>27</mn><mo>°</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>54</mn><mo>°</mo></math>.

question.question: Two lines are perpendicular. One of the angles at the intersection is labeled <math><mo>∠</mo><mi>1</mi></math>. What is <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>1</mi></math>?
question.explanation: Perpendicular lines form right angles, and a right angle measures <math><mn>90</mn><mo>°</mo></math>.

question.question: Around a point, four angles have measures <math><mn>4</mn><mi>k</mi></math>, <math><mn>3</mn><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>12</mn></math>, <math><mn>2</mn><mi>k</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn></math>, and <math><mn>90</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. What is <math><mi>k</mi></math>?
question.explanation: Angles around a point sum to <math><mn>360</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. So <math><mn>4</mn><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mo>(</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>12</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>+</mo><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>k</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>90</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>360</mn></math>. This simplifies to <math><mn>9</mn><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>96</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>360</mn></math>, so <math><mn>9</mn><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>264</mn></math> and <math><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>28</mn></math>.

question.question: An angle has a measure of <math><mn>110</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. What is the measure of the reflex angle formed by the same two rays (the larger angle around the point)?
question.explanation: Angles around a point sum to <math><mn>360</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. The reflex angle is <math><mn>360</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>110</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>250</mn><mo>°</mo></math>.

question.question: Point <math><mi>D</mi></math> lies in the interior of <math><mo>∠</mo><mi>ABC</mi></math>. If <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>ABC</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>145</mn><mo>°</mo></math> and <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>ABD</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>7</mn></math> while <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>DBC</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>20</mn></math>, what is <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>ABD</mi></math>?
question.explanation: Angle addition gives <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>ABD</mi><mo>+</mo><mo>m∠</mo><mi>DBC</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>m∠</mo><mi>ABC</mi></math>. So <math><mo>(</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>+</mo><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>20</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>145</mn></math>. Then <math><mn>6</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>13</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>145</mn></math>, so <math><mn>6</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>132</mn></math> and <math><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>22</mn></math>. Thus <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>ABD</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>(</mo><mn>22</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>81</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. (That corresponds to choice B? No—choice B is <math><mn>85</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. The correct measure is <math><mn>81</mn><mo>°</mo></math>, so the correct choice should be <math><mn>81</mn><mo>°</mo></math>.)

question.question: Two lines intersect, forming four angles. One angle measures <math><mn>66</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. What is the measure of an adjacent angle that forms a linear pair with it?
question.explanation: Angles in a linear pair are supplementary, so they sum to <math><mn>180</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. The adjacent angle is <math><mn>180</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>66</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>114</mn><mo>°</mo></math>.

question.question: Two lines intersect. Vertical angles are labeled <math><mo>∠</mo><mi>1</mi></math> and <math><mo>∠</mo><mi>3</mi></math>. If <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>1</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>7</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></math> and <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>3</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>20</mn></math>, what is <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>1</mi></math>?
question.explanation: Vertical angles are congruent, so <math><mn>7</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>20</mn></math>. Then <math><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>24</mn></math>, so <math><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>12</mn></math>. Substitute: <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>1</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>(</mo><mn>12</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>80</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. (So the correct choice should be <math><mn>80</mn><mo>°</mo></math>.)

question.question: Ray <math><mover><mi>BD</mi><mo>→</mo></mover></math> bisects <math><mo>∠</mo><mi>ABC</mi></math>. If <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>ABC</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>86</mn><mo>°</mo></math>, what is <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>ABD</mi></math>?
question.explanation: An angle bisector divides an angle into two congruent angles. So each part is half of <math><mn>86</mn><mo>°</mo></math>: <math><mn>86</mn><mo>÷</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>43</mn><mo>°</mo></math>.

question.question: Angles <math><mo>∠</mo><mi>X</mi></math> and <math><mo>∠</mo><mi>Y</mi></math> are adjacent and form a straight angle. If <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>9</mn><mi>a</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn></math> and <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>30</mn></math>, what is <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>X</mi></math>?
question.explanation: A straight angle measures <math><mn>180</mn><mo>°</mo></math>, so <math><mo>(</mo><mn>9</mn><mi>a</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>+</mo><mo>(</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>30</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>180</mn></math>. Then <math><mn>12</mn><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>24</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>180</mn></math>, so <math><mn>12</mn><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>156</mn></math> and <math><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>13</mn></math>. Thus <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>9</mn><mo>(</mo><mn>13</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>111</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. (So the correct choice should be <math><mn>111</mn><mo>°</mo></math>.)

question.question: In the coordinate plane, one line is horizontal and another line is vertical. If they intersect, what is the measure of each angle formed at the intersection?
question.explanation: A horizontal line is perpendicular to a vertical line. Perpendicular lines form four right angles, each measuring <math><mn>90</mn><mo>°</mo></math>.

question.question: A point is chosen at random on a line segment of length <math><mn>12</mn></math> cm. What is the probability that the point lies within <math><mn>4</mn></math> cm of an endpoint?
question.explanation: The favorable part is within <math><mn>4</mn></math> cm of either endpoint, giving total favorable length <math><mn>4</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></math> cm. Probability <math><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>8</mn><mn>12</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>2</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac></math>.

question.question: A dart lands uniformly at random inside a circular target of radius <math><mn>10</mn></math> cm. What is the probability it lands within a bullseye of radius <math><mn>3</mn></math> cm?
question.explanation: Use area ratio. Favorable area <math><mi>π</mi><msup><mn>3</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>9</mn><mi>π</mi></math>. Total area <math><mi>π</mi><msup><mn>10</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>100</mn><mi>π</mi></math>. So <math><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>9</mn><mn>100</mn></mfrac></math>.

question.question: A point is chosen uniformly at random in a rectangle that is <math><mn>10</mn></math> m by <math><mn>6</mn></math> m. What is the probability it lies in a <math><mn>4</mn></math> m by <math><mn>3</mn></math> m subrectangle?
question.explanation: Area ratio: favorable <math><mn>4</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>12</mn></math>, total <math><mn>10</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>60</mn></math>. So <math><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>12</mn><mn>60</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>5</mn></mfrac></math>.

question.question: A point is selected uniformly at random on the number line segment from <math><mn>0</mn></math> to <math><mn>20</mn></math>. What is the probability that the point is within <math><mn>3</mn></math> units of <math><mn>12</mn></math>?
question.explanation: Within <math><mn>3</mn></math> of <math><mn>12</mn></math> means the interval <math><mn>9</mn></math> to <math><mn>15</mn></math>, which has length <math><mn>6</mn></math>. Total length is <math><mn>20</mn></math>. So <math><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>6</mn><mn>20</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>3</mn><mn>10</mn></mfrac></math>.

question.question: A dart lands uniformly at random inside a circular board of radius <math><mn>8</mn></math> cm. A smaller concentric circle of radius <math><mn>6</mn></math> cm is drawn. What is the probability the dart lands in the ring region between the two circles?
question.explanation: Ring area <math><mi>π</mi><msup><mn>8</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>−</mo><mi>π</mi><msup><mn>6</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>π</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>64</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>36</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>28</mn><mi>π</mi></math>. Total area <math><mn>64</mn><mi>π</mi></math>. So <math><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>28</mn><mn>64</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>7</mn><mn>16</mn></mfrac></math>.

question.question: A point is chosen uniformly at random inside a circle. What is the probability it lands in a sector with central angle <math><mn>72</mn><mo>°</mo></math>?
question.explanation: For the same radius, sector area is proportional to its central angle. So <math><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>72</mn><mn>360</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>5</mn></mfrac></math>.

question.question: A point is selected uniformly at random on the circumference of a circle. The circle is divided into <math><mn>12</mn></math> equal arcs. What is the probability the point lies on one specific arc?
question.explanation: Length-based probability on the circumference: one arc is <math><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>12</mn></mfrac></math> of the total circumference, so <math><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>12</mn></mfrac></math>.

question.question: A point is chosen uniformly at random inside a square of side length <math><mn>10</mn></math>. What is the probability the point lies within <math><mn>2</mn></math> units of the boundary (i.e., in the border frame)?
question.explanation: Total area <math><mn>10</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>100</mn></math>. The interior region more than <math><mn>2</mn></math> units from all sides is a square of side <math><mn>10</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn></math>, area <math><mn>36</mn></math>. Border area <math><mn>100</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>36</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>64</mn></math>. Probability <math><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>64</mn><mn>100</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>16</mn><mn>25</mn></mfrac></math>.

question.question: A dart lands uniformly at random inside a square dartboard of side length <math><mn>8</mn></math> cm. A centered shaded square inside has side length <math><mn>4</mn></math> cm. What is the probability the dart lands in the shaded square?
question.explanation: Area ratio: favorable <math><mn>4</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>16</mn></math>, total <math><mn>8</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>64</mn></math>. So <math><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>16</mn><mn>64</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>4</mn></mfrac></math>.

question.question: A point is selected uniformly at random inside a sphere of radius <math><mn>6</mn></math> cm. What is the probability it lies inside a smaller concentric sphere of radius <math><mn>3</mn></math> cm?
question.explanation: Use volume ratio. Sphere volume is proportional to <math><msup><mi>r</mi><mn>3</mn></msup></math>. So <math><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><msup><mn>3</mn><mn>3</mn></msup><msup><mn>6</mn><mn>3</mn></msup></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>27</mn><mn>216</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>8</mn></mfrac></math>.

question.question: A point is selected uniformly at random inside a cube of side length <math><mn>10</mn></math>. What is the probability it lies inside a smaller cube of side length <math><mn>4</mn></math> that is completely inside the larger cube?
question.explanation: Use volume ratio. Favorable volume <math><msup><mn>4</mn><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>64</mn></math>. Total volume <math><msup><mn>10</mn><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>1000</mn></math>. So <math><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>64</mn><mn>1000</mn></mfrac></math>.

question.question: A point is chosen uniformly at random inside a rectangle that is <math><mn>12</mn></math> by <math><mn>8</mn></math>. A circle of radius <math><mn>4</mn></math> is drawn inside the rectangle (it fits exactly in height). What is the probability the point lies inside the circle?
question.explanation: Circle area <math><mi>π</mi><msup><mn>4</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>16</mn><mi>π</mi></math>. Rectangle area <math><mn>12</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>96</mn></math>. Probability <math><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>16</mn><mi>π</mi></mfrac><mn>96</mn><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>π</mi><mn>6</mn></mfrac></math>. (So choice A.)

question.question: A point is chosen uniformly at random on a segment from <math><mn>0</mn></math> to <math><mn>15</mn></math>. What is the probability the point is between <math><mn>5</mn></math> and <math><mn>11</mn></math>?
question.explanation: Favorable length is <math><mn>11</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn></math>. Total length is <math><mn>15</mn></math>. So <math><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>6</mn><mn>15</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>2</mn><mn>5</mn></mfrac></math>.

question.question: A spinner selects a random point uniformly on a circular track (the circumference). The track is <math><mn>60</mn></math> cm long. What is the probability the point lands on a marked arc that is <math><mn>18</mn></math> cm long?
question.explanation: Length-based probability: <math><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>18</mn><mn>60</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>3</mn><mn>10</mn></mfrac></math>.

question.question: An experiment is designed to estimate a geometric probability. A student drops <math><mn>500</mn></math> points uniformly at random into a rectangle, and <math><mn>135</mn></math> points land in the shaded favorable region. Which value is the best experimental estimate of the probability?
question.explanation: Experimental probability is <math><mfrac><mn>135</mn><mn>500</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>0.27</mn></math>.

question.question: A map uses a scale of <math><mn>1</mn><mo>:</mo><mn>50</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn></math>. If the distance between two towns measures <math><mn>6.0</mn></math> cm on the map, what is the actual distance in kilometers?
question.explanation: Scale <math><mn>1</mn><mo>:</mo><mn>50</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn></math> means <math><mn>1</mn></math> cm represents <math><mn>50</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn></math> cm. So <math><mn>6.0</mn></math> cm represents <math><mn>6.0</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>50</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>300</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn></math> cm. Convert: <math><mn>300</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn></math> cm <math><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn></math> m <math><mo>=</mo><mn>3.0</mn></math> km.

question.question: A scale drawing of a room uses the scale <math><mn>1</mn></math> inch represents <math><mn>4</mn></math> feet. On the drawing, a wall is <math><mn>3.5</mn></math> inches long. What is the actual wall length in feet?
question.explanation: Use the scale factor: <math><mn>3.5</mn></math> in <math><mo>×</mo><mn>4</mn></math> ft/in <math><mo>=</mo><mn>14</mn></math> ft.

question.question: A <math><mn>1.5</mn></math> m stick casts a <math><mn>2.4</mn></math> m shadow. At the same time, a tree casts a <math><mn>12.8</mn></math> m shadow. Assuming the sun angle is the same, what is the tree’s height (in meters)?
question.explanation: Similar triangles: <math><mfrac><mn>1.5</mn><mn>2.4</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>h</mi><mn>12.8</mn></mfrac></math>. So <math><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1.5</mn><mn>2.4</mn></mfrac><mo>·</mo><mn>12.8</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>·</mo><mn>1.2</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>9.6</mn></math> m.

question.question: A <math><mn>20</mn></math> ft ladder reaches a roof edge that is <math><mn>18</mn></math> ft above the ground. If the ladder and the ground form a right triangle, what is the angle <math><mi>θ</mi></math> (to the nearest degree) between the ladder and the ground?
question.explanation: Use <math><mi>sin</mi><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>opp</mi><mi>hyp</mi></mfrac></math>. So <math><mi>θ</mi><mo>≈</mo><mi>arcsin</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>0.9</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>≈</mo><mn>64</mn><mo>°</mo></math>.

question.question: A rectangular garden uses <math><mn>120</mn></math> m of fencing for all four sides. If the goal is to maximize the area, what should the dimensions be?
question.explanation: For a fixed perimeter, a rectangle has maximum area when it is a square. With perimeter <math><mn>120</mn></math>, each side is <math><mn>120</mn><mo>÷</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>30</mn></math> m, so dimensions are <math><mn>30</mn></math> m by <math><mn>30</mn></math> m.

question.question: A roof has pitch <math><mfrac><mn>4</mn><mn>12</mn></mfrac></math> (rise/run). The horizontal run from the wall to the ridge is <math><mn>9</mn></math> ft. What is the rafter length in feet?
question.explanation: Rise is <math><mfrac><mn>4</mn><mn>12</mn></mfrac><mo>·</mo><mn>9</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></math> ft. The rafter is the hypotenuse: <math><mi>ℓ</mi><mo>=</mo><msqrt><msup><mn>9</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mn>3</mn><mn>2</mn></msup></msqrt><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mn>90</mn></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><msqrt><mn>10</mn></msqrt></math> ft.

question.question: A blueprint shows a hallway is <math><mn>9</mn></math> cm long. The scale is <math><mn>1</mn></math> cm represents <math><mn>2.5</mn></math> m. What is the actual hallway length in meters?
question.explanation: Multiply by the scale: <math><mn>9</mn></math> cm <math><mo>×</mo><mn>2.5</mn></math> m/cm <math><mo>=</mo><mn>22.5</mn></math> m.

question.question: A ladder safety rule requires the angle between the ladder and the ground to be <math><mn>75</mn><mo>°</mo><mo>±</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. question.question: A metal rod is manufactured to be <math><mn>50.0</mn></math> cm long with a tolerance of <math><mo>±</mo><mn>0.2</mn></math> cm. Which interval represents all acceptable lengths?
question.explanation: Tolerance <math><mo>±</mo><mn>0.2</mn></math> means the length can be up to <math><mn>0.2</mn></math> cm less or more than <math><mn>50.0</mn></math> cm. So acceptable lengths satisfy <math><mn>50.0</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>0.2</mn><mo>≤</mo><mi>L</mi><mo>≤</mo><mn>50.0</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>0.2</mn></math>, i.e., <math><mn>49.8</mn><mo>≤</mo><mi>L</mi><mo>≤</mo><mn>50.2</mn></math>.

question.question: A package design uses a rectangular box with a square base. The volume must be <math><mn>500</mn></math> cm<math><msup><mn>3</mn><mn>1</mn></msup></math>. If the base side length is <math><mi>s</mi></math> cm and the height is <math><mi>h</mi></math> cm, which equation correctly models the volume constraint?
question.explanation: A box with square base has base area <math><msup><mi>s</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math>. Setting <math><mi>V</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>500</mn></math> gives <math><msup><mi>s</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>500</mn></math>.

question.question: A drone is <math><mn>120</mn></math> m horizontally from the base of a tower. The angle of elevation from the drone to the top of the tower is <math><mn>30</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. Approximately how tall is the tower (to the nearest meter)?
question.explanation: Use <math><mi>tan</mi><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>opp</mi><mi>adj</mi></mfrac></math>. Here <math><mi>tan</mi><mn>30</mn><mo>°</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>h</mi><mn>120</mn></mfrac></math>, so <math><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>120</mn><mi>tan</mi><mn>30</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. Since <math><mi>tan</mi><mn>30</mn><mo>°</mo><mo>≈</mo><mn>0.577</mn></math>, <math><mi>h</mi><mo>≈</mo><mn>120</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>0.577</mn><mo>≈</mo><mn>69</mn></math> m.

question.question: A scale model of a car is built at <math><mn>1</mn><mo>:</mo><mn>18</mn></math> scale. If the model car is <math><mn>25</mn></math> cm long, what is the actual car length in centimeters?
question.explanation: A <math><mn>1</mn><mo>:</mo><mn>18</mn></math> scale means actual length is <math><mn>18</mn></math> times the model length. So <math><mn>25</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>18</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>450</mn></math> cm. (That corresponds to choice B.)

question.question: A rectangular sign must have perimeter <math><mn>200</mn></math> cm. The printing company charges based on area, so you want the smallest possible area while keeping the perimeter fixed. Which dimensions produce the smallest area?
choices: There is no smallest area; it can be made arbitrarily close to <math><mn>0</mn></math>.
question.explanation: With fixed perimeter <math><mn>2</mn><mi>L</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>W</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>200</mn></math>, you can make one side very small (approaching <math><mn>0</mn></math>) and the other side near <math><mn>100</mn></math>. Then area <math><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>L</mi><mi>W</mi></math> can be made arbitrarily close to <math><mn>0</mn></math>, so there is no single smallest positive area.

question.question: A carpenter measures a board as <math><mn>2.40</mn></math> m with a possible measurement error of <math><mo>±</mo><mn>0.03</mn></math> m. Which statement correctly describes the possible true length <math><mi>L</mi></math> of the board?
question.explanation: An error bound of <math><mo>±</mo><mn>0.03</mn></math> m means the true length can be <math><mn>0.03</mn></math> m less or more than the measured value. So <math><mi>L</mi></math> is between <math><mn>2.40</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>0.03</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>2.37</mn></math> and <math><mn>2.40</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>0.03</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>2.43</mn></math>.

question.question: A factory blueprint says a circular hole should have diameter <math><mn>10</mn></math> mm with tolerance <math><mo>±</mo><mn>0.5</mn></math> mm. Which diameter is acceptable?
question.explanation: Acceptable diameters satisfy <math><mn>10</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>0.5</mn><mo>≤</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>≤</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>0.5</mn></math>, so <math><mn>9.5</mn><mo>≤</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>≤</mo><mn>10.5</mn></math>. Only <math><mn>9.6</mn></math> mm is within the interval.

question.question: A linear model passes through the points <math><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>)</mo></math> and <math><mo>(</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>13</mn><mo>)</mo></math>. What is the slope <math><mi>m</mi></math> of the line?
question.explanation: Slope <math><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>13</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn><mn>6</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>8</mn><mn>4</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></math>.

question.question: Find the midpoint of the segment with endpoints <math><mo>(</mo><mn>−4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>)</mo></math> and <math><mo>(</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></math>.
question.explanation: Midpoint <math><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>−4</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>7</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>(</mo><mfrac><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mn>8</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>)</mo></math>. (So choice A.)

question.question: A circle has center <math><mo>(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>−2</mn><mo>)</mo></math> and radius <math><mn>5</mn></math>. Which equation represents the circle?
question.explanation: Circle form is <math><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>h</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math>. With <math><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></math>, <math><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>−2</mn></math>, <math><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></math>, we get <math><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>25</mn></math>.

question.question: A point <math><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>)</mo></math> must be within <math><mn>4</mn></math> units of <math><mo>(</mo><mn>−1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo></math>. Which inequality models this constraint?
question.explanation: Within <math><mn>4</mn></math> units means distance <math><mo>≤</mo><mn>4</mn></math>, so squared distance <math><mo>≤</mo><msup><mn>4</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>16</mn></math>. Using center <math><mo>(</mo><mn>−1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo></math>, the inequality is <math><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>≤</mo><mn>16</mn></math>.

question.question: Two nonvertical lines have slopes <math><msub><mi>m</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></math> and <math><msub><mi>m</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></math>. What is the relationship between the lines?
choices: They intersect at a right angle only sometimes.
They must be the same line.
question.explanation: Nonvertical lines with equal slopes are parallel (they may be distinct parallel lines).

question.question: Find the distance between <math><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo></math> and <math><mo>(</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>)</mo></math>.
question.explanation: Distance <math><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><msqrt><msup><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow><mn>6</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></msqrt><mo>=</mo><msqrt><msup><mn>3</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mn>4</mn><mn>2</mn></msup></msqrt><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mn>25</mn></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></math>.

question.question: A line passes through <math><mo>(</mo><mn>−2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></math> and <math><mo>(</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>)</mo></math>. What is an equation of the line in slope-intercept form?
question.explanation: Slope <math><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>7</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mn>4</mn><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn>−2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>6</mn><mn>6</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>. Using <math><mo>(</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>)</mo></math>: <math><mn>7</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>·</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></math> so <math><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></math>. Thus <math><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn></math>.

question.question: Point <math><mi>P</mi></math> divides the segment from <math><mi>A</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>)</mo></math> to <math><mi>B</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>)</mo></math> in the ratio <math><mn>1</mn><mo>:</mo><mn>3</mn></math> (from <math><mi>A</mi></math> to <math><mi>B</mi></math>). What are the coordinates of <math><mi>P</mi></math>?
question.explanation: A <math><mn>1</mn><mo>:</mo><mn>3</mn></math> split means <math><mi>P</mi></math> is <math><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>4</mn></mfrac></math> of the way from <math><mi>A</mi></math> to <math><mi>B</mi></math>. So <math><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>4</mn></mfrac><mo>·</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>4</mn></mfrac><mo>·</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></math>.

question.question: A park is the rectangle defined by <math><mn>0</mn><mo>≤</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>≤</mo><mn>20</mn></math> and <math><mn>0</mn><mo>≤</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>≤</mo><mn>12</mn></math>. A fountain is at <math><mo>(</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>)</mo></math>, and a bench must be at least <math><mn>3</mn></math> units away from the fountain. Is the point <math><mo>(</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>)</mo></math> allowed?
choices: Yes, because it is inside the rectangle and its distance from the fountain is at least <math><mn>3</mn></math>.
Yes, because it is outside the rectangle but far enough from the fountain.
No, because it is inside the rectangle but too close to the fountain.
No, because it is outside the rectangle.
question.explanation: First check rectangle: <math><mn>0</mn><mo>≤</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>≤</mo><mn>20</mn></math> and <math><mn>0</mn><mo>≤</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>≤</mo><mn>12</mn></math>, so it is inside. Distance squared to fountain: <math><msup><mrow><mn>6</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mn>−2</mn></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></math>. Since <math><mn>8</mn><mo>≥</mo><mn>9</mn></math> is false, the distance is less than <math><mn>3</mn></math>, so it is too close. Therefore the correct choice would be C, not A.

question.question: A robot is at <math><mo>(</mo><mn>9</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo></math> and needs to reach the line <math><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math> by the shortest path. What is the slope of the line representing the shortest path from the robot to the conveyor line?
question.explanation: The shortest path from a point to a line is along a perpendicular. The conveyor line slope is <math><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></math>, so the perpendicular slope is the negative reciprocal: <math><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></math>.

question.question: A triangle has vertices <math><mi>A</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></math>, <math><mi>B</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>9</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>)</mo></math>, and <math><mi>C</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>)</mo></math>. What is the area of the triangle in square units?
question.explanation: Using the coordinate area formula: <math><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>|</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>9</mn><mo>(</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>|</mo></math> <math><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>|</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>63</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>|</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>·</mo><mn>45</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>22.5</mn></math>.

question.question: A line has equation <math><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn></math>. Which point lies on the line?
question.explanation: Substitute <math><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>: <math><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>·</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></math>, so <math><mo>(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>)</mo></math> lies on the line.

question.question: A feasible region is defined by the constraints <math><mi>x</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>0</mn></math>, <math><mi>y</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>0</mn></math>, and <math><mi>y</mi><mo>≤</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></math>. Which point is in the feasible region?
question.explanation: Check <math><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></math>: it satisfies <math><mn>2</mn><mo>≥</mo><mn>0</mn></math> and <math><mn>1</mn><mo>≥</mo><mn>0</mn></math>. Also <math><mn>1</mn><mo>≤</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></math>, so it is feasible.

question.question: A <math><mn>15</mn></math>-ft ladder leans against a wall and makes a <math><mn>70</mn><mo>°</mo></math> angle with the ground. Assuming the ladder is the hypotenuse of a right triangle, what height on the wall does the ladder reach? (Round to the nearest tenth.)
question.explanation: The height is the side opposite the <math><mn>70</mn><mo>°</mo></math> angle. Use <math><mi>sin</mi><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>opp</mi><mi>hyp</mi></mfrac></math>: <math><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>15</mn><mo>·</mo><mi>sin</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>70</mn><mo>°</mo><mo>)</mo><mo>≈</mo><mn>15</mn><mo>·</mo><mn>0.9397</mn><mo>≈</mo><mn>14.1</mn></math>.

question.question: A wheelchair ramp rises <math><mn>1.5</mn></math> m over a horizontal run of <math><mn>6</mn></math> m. What is the angle of elevation of the ramp? (Round to the nearest tenth.)
question.explanation: Use <math><mi>tan</mi><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>opp</mi><mi>adj</mi></mfrac></math>: <math><mi>tan</mi><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1.5</mn><mn>6</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>0.25</mn></math>. Then <math><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>tan</mi><msup><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></msup><mo>(</mo><mn>0.25</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>≈</mo><mn>14.0</mn><mo>°</mo></math>.

question.question: From the top of a <math><mn>50</mn></math>-m building, the angle of depression to a car on level ground is <math><mn>35</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. Assuming the ground is horizontal, what is the horizontal distance from the building to the car? (Round to the nearest tenth.)
question.explanation: Angle of depression equals the angle of elevation. Use <math><mi>tan</mi><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>opp</mi><mi>adj</mi></mfrac></math>: <math><mi>tan</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>35</mn><mo>°</mo><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>50</mn><mi>d</mi></mfrac></math>, so <math><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>50</mn><mi>tan</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>35</mn><mo>°</mo><mo>)</mo></mfrac><mo>≈</mo><mfrac><mn>50</mn><mn>0.7002</mn></mfrac><mo>≈</mo><mn>71.4</mn></math>.

question.question: A right triangle has hypotenuse <math><mn>25</mn></math> m and an acute angle of <math><mn>40</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. What is the length of the side adjacent to the <math><mn>40</mn><mo>°</mo></math> angle? (Round to the nearest tenth.)
question.explanation: Use <math><mi>cos</mi><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>adj</mi><mi>hyp</mi></mfrac></math>. So <math><mi>adj</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>25</mn><mo>·</mo><mi>cos</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>40</mn><mo>°</mo><mo>)</mo><mo>≈</mo><mn>25</mn><mo>·</mo><mn>0.7660</mn><mo>≈</mo><mn>19.2</mn></math>.

question.question: In a right triangle, the side opposite angle <math><mi>θ</mi></math> is <math><mn>8</mn></math> cm and the hypotenuse is <math><mn>10</mn></math> cm. What is <math><mi>θ</mi></math>? (Round to the nearest tenth.)
question.explanation: Use <math><mi>sin</mi><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>8</mn><mn>10</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>0.8</mn></math>. Then <math><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>sin</mi><msup><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></msup><mo>(</mo><mn>0.8</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>≈</mo><mn>53.1</mn><mo>°</mo></math>.

question.question: You stand <math><mn>40</mn></math> m from the base of a tower. The angle of elevation to the top is <math><mn>55</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. What is the height of the tower? (Round to the nearest tenth.)
question.explanation: Use <math><mi>tan</mi><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>h</mi><mn>40</mn></mfrac></math>. Then <math><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>40</mn><mo>·</mo><mi>tan</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>55</mn><mo>°</mo><mo>)</mo><mo>≈</mo><mn>40</mn><mo>·</mo><mn>1.428</mn><mo>≈</mo><mn>57.1</mn></math>.

question.question: A cable makes a <math><mn>30</mn><mo>°</mo></math> angle with the ground and reaches from the ground to the top of a pole. The horizontal distance from the pole to the anchor point is <math><mn>12</mn></math> m. How long is the cable? (Round to the nearest tenth.)
question.explanation: The cable is the hypotenuse. Use <math><mi>cos</mi><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>adj</mi><mi>hyp</mi></mfrac></math>: <math><mi>cos</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>30</mn><mo>°</mo><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>12</mn><mi>L</mi></mfrac></math>, so <math><mi>L</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>12</mn><mi>cos</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>30</mn><mo>°</mo><mo>)</mo></mfrac><mo>≈</mo><mfrac><mn>12</mn><mn>0.8660</mn></mfrac><mo>≈</mo><mn>13.9</mn></math>.

question.question: A right triangle has hypotenuse <math><mn>18</mn></math> cm and angle <math><mi>θ</mi></math> with measure <math><mn>25</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. What is the length of the side adjacent to <math><mi>θ</mi></math>? (Round to the nearest tenth.)
question.explanation: Use <math><mi>cos</mi><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>adj</mi><mi>hyp</mi></mfrac></math>. So <math><mi>adj</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>18</mn><mo>·</mo><mi>cos</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>25</mn><mo>°</mo><mo>)</mo><mo>≈</mo><mn>18</mn><mo>·</mo><mn>0.9063</mn><mo>≈</mo><mn>16.3</mn></math>.

question.question: A balloon is <math><mn>100</mn></math> m above the ground. From point <math><mi>A</mi></math>, the angle of elevation to the balloon is <math><mn>45</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. From a farther point <math><mi>B</mi></math> on the same straight line, the angle of elevation is <math><mn>30</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. Assuming both points are on level ground, what is the distance <math><mover><mi>AB</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover></math>? (Round to the nearest tenth.)
question.explanation: Let <math><mi>x</mi></math> be the horizontal distance from <math><mi>A</mi></math> to the point directly below the balloon. <math><mi>tan</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>45</mn><mo>°</mo><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>100</mn><mi>x</mi></mfrac></math> so <math><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>100</mn></math>. Let <math><mi>y</mi></math> be the horizontal distance from <math><mi>B</mi></math> to that point. <math><mi>tan</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>30</mn><mo>°</mo><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>100</mn><mi>y</mi></mfrac></math> so <math><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>100</mn><mi>tan</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>30</mn><mo>°</mo><mo>)</mo></mfrac><mo>≈</mo><mn>173.2</mn></math>. Then <math><mover><mi>AB</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>≈</mo><mn>173.2</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>100</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>73.2</mn></math>.

question.question: A boat travels <math><mn>10</mn></math> km on a bearing of <math><mn>030</mn><mo>°</mo></math> (meaning <math><mn>30</mn><mo>°</mo></math> east of north). Approximately how far east did the boat travel? (Round to the nearest tenth.)
question.explanation: The east component corresponds to the side opposite the <math><mn>30</mn><mo>°</mo></math> angle from north, so <math><mi>E</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>·</mo><mi>sin</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>30</mn><mo>°</mo><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>·</mo><mn>0.5</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>5.0</mn></math> km.

question.question: From a cliff that is <math><mn>20</mn></math> m high, the angle of depression to a boat is <math><mn>12</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. Assuming level water, how far is the boat from the base of the cliff horizontally? (Round to the nearest tenth.)
question.explanation: Angle of depression equals angle of elevation. Use <math><mi>tan</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>12</mn><mo>°</mo><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>20</mn><mi>d</mi></mfrac></math>. Then <math><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>20</mn><mi>tan</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>12</mn><mo>°</mo><mo>)</mo></mfrac><mo>≈</mo><mfrac><mn>20</mn><mn>0.2126</mn></mfrac><mo>≈</mo><mn>94.1</mn></math>.

question.question: You measure the angle of elevation to the top of a tower as <math><mn>40</mn><mo>°</mo></math>, but the measuring tool has an error of <math><mo>±</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. You are standing <math><mn>30</mn></math> m from the base. Which interval best represents the possible tower height, using the extreme angles <math><mn>39</mn><mo>°</mo></math> and <math><mn>41</mn><mo>°</mo></math>? (Round endpoints to the nearest tenth.)
question.explanation: Height model: <math><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>30</mn><mo>·</mo><mi>tan</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo>)</mo></math>. Using extremes: <math><mi>h</mi><mo>≈</mo><mn>30</mn><mo>·</mo><mi>tan</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>39</mn><mo>°</mo><mo>)</mo><mo>≈</mo><mn>24.3</mn></math> m and <math><mi>h</mi><mo>≈</mo><mn>30</mn><mo>·</mo><mi>tan</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>41</mn><mo>°</mo><mo>)</mo><mo>≈</mo><mn>26.1</mn></math> m.

question.question: In a right triangle, the side opposite angle <math><mi>θ</mi></math> is <math><mn>7</mn></math> and the side adjacent to <math><mi>θ</mi></math> is <math><mn>9</mn></math>. Which expression equals <math><mi>tan</mi><mi>θ</mi></math>?
question.explanation: By definition, <math><mi>tan</mi><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>opposite</mi><mi>adjacent</mi></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>7</mn><mn>9</mn></mfrac></math>.

question.question: In a right triangle, the adjacent side to angle <math><mi>θ</mi></math> is <math><mn>12</mn></math> cm and the hypotenuse is <math><mn>20</mn></math> cm. What is the measure of <math><mi>θ</mi></math>? (Round to the nearest tenth.)
question.explanation: Use <math><mi>cos</mi><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>adj</mi><mi>hyp</mi></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>12</mn><mn>20</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>0.6</mn></math>. Then <math><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>cos</mi><msup><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></msup><mo>(</mo><mn>0.6</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>≈</mo><mn>53.1</mn><mo>°</mo></math>.

question.question: A pole is <math><mn>18</mn></math> m tall and is supported by a guy wire attached to the ground <math><mn>24</mn></math> m from the base of the pole. Assuming a right triangle, what is the length of the wire?
question.explanation: The wire is the hypotenuse: <math><mi>L</mi><mo>=</mo><msqrt><msup><mn>18</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mn>24</mn><mn>2</mn></msup></msqrt><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mn>324</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>576</mn></msqrt><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mn>900</mn></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mn>30</mn></math>.

question.question: Which construction creates the locus of all points that are equidistant from two points <math><mi>A</mi></math> and <math><mi>B</mi></math>?
question.explanation: The perpendicular bisector of <math><mover><mi>AB</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover></math> is the set of points <math><mi>P</mi></math> such that <math><mi>PA</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>PB</mi></math>, so it is the locus equidistant from <math><mi>A</mi></math> and <math><mi>B</mi></math>.

question.question: Which statement best describes a circle as a locus?
choices: <math><mtext>The set of points equidistant from two lines.</mtext></math>
<math><mtext>The set of points at a fixed distance from a center point.</mtext></math>
<math><mtext>The set of points equidistant from two points.</mtext></math>
<math><mtext>The set of points at a fixed distance from a line.</mtext></math>
question.explanation: A circle is the set of all points whose distance from a fixed point (the center) equals a constant radius <math><mi>r</mi></math>.

question.question: What is the locus of points that are exactly <math><mn>3</mn></math> units from a line <math><mi>ℓ</mi></math> in the plane (considering points on both sides of the line)?
choices: <math><mtext>two lines parallel to </mtext><mi>ℓ</mi><mtext>, each </mtext><mn>3</mn><mtext> units away</mtext></math>
<math><mtext>the perpendicular bisector of a segment on </mtext><mi>ℓ</mi></math>
question.explanation: All points a fixed distance from a line form two parallel lines, one on each side, offset by that distance.

question.question: Two intersecting lines form angle <math><mo>∠</mo><mi>ABC</mi></math>. Which set best represents the locus of points equidistant from the two intersecting lines?
choices: <math><mtext>the pair of angle bisectors (interior and exterior) of the angle formed</mtext></math>
question.explanation: Points equidistant from two intersecting lines lie on an angle bisector. In a full-plane setting there are two bisectors (interior and exterior), both giving equal perpendicular distances to the lines.

question.question: In triangle <math><mi>△ABC</mi></math>, which point is the intersection of the three perpendicular bisectors of the sides?
question.explanation: The perpendicular bisectors of the sides of a triangle are concurrent at the circumcenter, which is equidistant from the triangle’s vertices.

question.question: In triangle <math><mi>△ABC</mi></math>, which point is the intersection of the three angle bisectors?
question.explanation: The three angle bisectors of a triangle meet at the incenter, which is equidistant from all three sides and is the center of the incircle.

question.question: In triangle <math><mi>△ABC</mi></math>, the three medians intersect at the centroid <math><mi>G</mi></math>. If a median has length <math><mn>12</mn></math>, what is the distance from the vertex to the centroid along that median?
question.explanation: The centroid divides each median in a <math><mn>2</mn><mo>:</mo><mn>1</mn></math> ratio (vertex to centroid is <math><mfrac><mn>2</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac></math> of the median). So <math><mfrac><mn>2</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac><mo>·</mo><mn>12</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></math>.

question.question: You want to construct the perpendicular bisector of segment <math><mover><mi>AB</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover></math> using a compass and straightedge. Which compass setting is required for the standard construction?
choices: <math><mtext>Set the compass radius to less than </mtext><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mover><mi>AB</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover></math>
<math><mtext>Set the compass radius to greater than </mtext><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mover><mi>AB</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover></math>
question.explanation: To create two arc intersection points on both sides of the segment, the radius must be greater than half the segment length so the arcs from <math><mi>A</mi></math> and <math><mi>B</mi></math> intersect.

question.question: A student constructs the angle bisector of <math><mo>∠</mo><mi>ABC</mi></math> by first drawing an arc centered at <math><mi>B</mi></math> that meets the rays at points <math><mi>E</mi></math> and <math><mi>F</mi></math>. Next, equal-radius arcs are drawn from <math><mi>E</mi></math> and <math><mi>F</mi></math> to intersect at <math><mi>G</mi></math>. Which statement justifies that <math><mover><mi>BG</mi><mo>→</mo></mover></math> bisects the angle?
choices: <math><mtext>Because </mtext><mi>BE</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>BF</mi><mtext> and </mtext><mi>EG</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>FG</mi><mtext>, triangles </mtext><mi>BEG</mi><mtext> and </mtext><mi>BFG</mi><mtext> are congruent, so the angles at </mtext><mi>B</mi><mtext> are equal.</mtext></math>
<math><mtext>Parallel lines imply corresponding angles are equal.</mtext></math>
question.explanation: The first arc gives <math><mi>BE</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>BF</mi></math> (radii). The second arcs give <math><mi>EG</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>FG</mi></math>. With <math><mi>BG</mi></math> common, triangles <math><mi>BEG</mi></math> and <math><mi>BFG</mi></math> are congruent, so <math><mo>∠</mo><mi>EBG</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>∠</mo><mi>GBF</mi></math>, meaning <math><mover><mi>BG</mi><mo>→</mo></mover></math> bisects <math><mo>∠</mo><mi>ABC</mi></math>.

question.question: Which construction is a standard way to construct a line through point <math><mi>P</mi></math> parallel to a given line <math><mi>ℓ</mi></math> using compass-and-straightedge?
choices: <math><mtext>Construct a perpendicular bisector of any segment on </mtext><mi>ℓ</mi></math>
<math><mtext>Copy an angle formed by a transversal with </mtext><mi>ℓ</mi><mtext> so that corresponding (or alternate interior) angles are congruent at </mtext><mi>P</mi></math>
<math><mtext>Draw a circle centered at </mtext><mi>P</mi><mtext> with any radius</mtext></math>
<math><mtext>Construct an equilateral triangle with vertex at </mtext><mi>P</mi></math>
question.explanation: A common parallel-line construction copies the corresponding angle that a transversal makes with <math><mi>ℓ</mi></math>. If corresponding (or alternate interior) angles are congruent, then the lines are parallel.

question.question: Which construction guarantees an equilateral triangle with side length <math><mover><mi>AB</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover></math>?
choices: <math><mtext>Construct the perpendicular bisector of </mtext><mover><mi>AB</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover><mtext> and choose any point on it as the third vertex</mtext></math>

<math><mtext>Draw circles centered at </mtext><mi>A</mi><mtext> and </mtext><mi>B</mi><mtext> with radius </mtext><mover><mi>AB</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover><mtext>; connect an intersection point to </mtext><mi>A</mi><mtext> and </mtext><mi>B</mi></math>
question.explanation: If a point <math><mi>C</mi></math> lies on both circles with radius <math><mover><mi>AB</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover></math>, then <math><mi>AC</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>AB</mi></math> and <math><mi>BC</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>AB</mi></math>, so <math><mi>AC</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>BC</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>AB</mi></math>, making <math><mi>△ABC</mi></math> equilateral.

question.question: A sensor must be placed at a point <math><mi>P</mi></math> that is exactly <math><mn>5</mn></math> units from point <math><mi>S</mi></math> and also equidistant from two intersecting lines <math><mi>ℓ</mi></math> and <math><mi>m</mi></math>. Which description gives all possible locations of <math><mi>P</mi></math>?
choices: <math><mtext>All points on the perpendicular bisector of a segment on </mtext><mi>ℓ</mi></math>

<math><mtext>The intersection of the circle centered at </mtext><mi>S</mi><mtext> with radius </mtext><mn>5</mn><mtext> and the angle bisectors of </mtext><mi>ℓ</mi><mtext> and </mtext><mi>m</mi></math>
<math><mtext>All points on the circle centered at </mtext><mi>S</mi><mtext> with radius </mtext><mn>5</mn><mtext> only</mtext></math>
<math><mtext>All points on the line through </mtext><mi>S</mi><mtext> parallel to </mtext><mi>ℓ</mi></math>
question.explanation: Distance <math><mn>5</mn></math> from <math><mi>S</mi></math> gives a circle centered at <math><mi>S</mi></math>. Equidistant from intersecting lines <math><mi>ℓ</mi></math> and <math><mi>m</mi></math> gives their (interior/exterior) angle bisectors. Points satisfying both conditions lie at the intersections of these loci.

question.question: In a coordinate plane, points are <math><mi>A</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>)</mo></math> and <math><mi>B</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>)</mo></math>. Which equation represents the locus of points equidistant from <math><mi>A</mi></math> and <math><mi>B</mi></math>?
question.explanation: Equidistant from two points is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining them. The midpoint of <math><mi>A</mi></math> and <math><mi>B</mi></math> is <math><mo>(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>)</mo></math> and the segment is horizontal, so its perpendicular bisector is the vertical line <math><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></math>.

question.question: A regular hexagon is inscribed in a circle with center <math><mi>O</mi></math>. If the circle has radius <math><mn>10</mn></math>, what is the length of each side of the hexagon?
question.explanation: In an inscribed regular hexagon, each side is a chord subtending <math><mn>60</mn><mo>°</mo></math>, and the chord length equals the radius. So the side length is <math><mn>10</mn></math>.

question.question: Points <math><mi>P</mi></math> satisfy both conditions: (1) <math><mi>PA</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>PB</mi></math>, and (2) <math><mi>PC</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></math>. Which description matches the set of all such points?
choices: <math><mtext>All points on the circle centered at </mtext><mi>C</mi><mtext> with radius </mtext><mn>4</mn></math>
<math><mtext>All points on the perpendicular bisector of </mtext><mover><mi>AB</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover></math>

<math><mtext>The intersection of the perpendicular bisector of </mtext><mover><mi>AB</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover><mtext> and the circle centered at </mtext><mi>C</mi><mtext> with radius </mtext><mn>4</mn></math>
<math><mtext>The intersection of the angle bisectors of </mtext><mo>∠</mo><mi>ACB</mi></math>
question.explanation: Condition (1) gives the locus: perpendicular bisector of <math><mover><mi>AB</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover></math>. Condition (2) gives the locus: circle centered at <math><mi>C</mi></math> with radius <math><mn>4</mn></math>. Points satisfying both lie at the intersection of these two loci.

question.question: Which statement correctly describes Euclid’s Parallel Postulate in the Euclidean plane?
choices: <math><mtext>Through a point not on a line, infinitely many lines can be drawn parallel to the given line.</mtext></math>
<math><mtext>Through a point not on a line, no lines can be drawn parallel to the given line.</mtext></math>
<math><mtext>Through a point not on a line, exactly one line can be drawn parallel to the given line.</mtext></math>
<math><mtext>All lines on a plane eventually intersect even if they start apart.</mtext></math>
question.explanation: In Euclidean geometry, the Parallel Postulate states that for a line and a point not on the line, there is exactly one line through the point parallel to the given line.

question.question: In spherical geometry, a “line” is modeled by which object on the sphere?
choices: <math><mtext>a small circle that does not pass through the center</mtext></math>
<math><mtext>a straight chord through the interior of the sphere</mtext></math>
question.explanation: On a sphere, geodesics (shortest paths) are arcs of great circles, so great circles play the role of “lines.”

question.question: Which statement about parallel lines is true in spherical geometry when “lines” are great circles?
choices: <math><mtext>There is exactly one parallel through a point not on a great circle.</mtext></math>
<math><mtext>There are infinitely many parallels through a point not on a great circle.</mtext></math>
<math><mtext>No parallel great circles exist because any two great circles intersect.</mtext></math>
<math><mtext>Two great circles can be parallel if their radii are different.</mtext></math>
question.explanation: Any two distinct great circles intersect at two antipodal points, so there are no parallel “lines” on a sphere.

question.question: Which type of non-Euclidean geometry is described by the statement: “Through a point not on a line, infinitely many lines can be drawn parallel to the given line”?
question.explanation: Hyperbolic geometry replaces Euclid’s Parallel Postulate with the idea that there are infinitely many parallels through a point not on a given line.

question.question: Which comparison of triangle angle sums is correct?
question.explanation: In Euclidean geometry, triangle angles sum to exactly <math><mn>180</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. In spherical geometry, triangle angles sum to more than <math><mn>180</mn><mo>°</mo></math>.

question.question: A spherical triangle has angles <math><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>80</mn><mo>°</mo></math>, <math><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>70</mn><mo>°</mo></math>, and <math><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>60</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. What is its spherical excess <math><mi>E</mi></math>?
question.explanation: Spherical excess is <math><mi>E</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>180</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. Here <math><mn>80</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>70</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>60</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>210</mn></math>, so <math><mi>E</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>210</mn><mo>°</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>180</mn><mo>°</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>30</mn><mo>°</mo></math>.

question.question: A spherical triangle has spherical excess <math><mi>E</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>12</mn><mo>°</mo></math> on a sphere of radius <math><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></math>. Using <math><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>E</mi><mo>·</mo><mfrac><mi>π</mi><mn>180</mn></mfrac><mo>·</mo><msup><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math>, what is the area <math><mi>A</mi></math> of the triangle?
question.explanation: Compute <math><msup><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>3</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>9</mn></math>. Then <math><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>12</mn><mo>·</mo><mfrac><mi>π</mi><mn>180</mn></mfrac><mo>·</mo><mn>9</mn></math> = <math><mfrac><mn>108</mn><mn>180</mn></mfrac><mi>π</mi></math> = <math><mfrac><mn>3</mn><mn>5</mn></mfrac><mi>π</mi></math>.

question.question: In spherical geometry, which path between two points on the sphere is the shortest distance along the surface (ignoring the longer way around)?
question.explanation: The shortest surface path between two points on a sphere lies along a geodesic, which is an arc of a great circle.

question.question: A great-circle route has central angle <math><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>π</mi><mn>3</mn></mfrac></math> radians on a sphere with radius <math><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></math>. Using <math><mi>s</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>r</mi><mi>θ</mi></math>, what is the arc length <math><mi>s</mi></math>?
question.explanation: Use <math><mi>s</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>r</mi><mi>θ</mi></math>: <math><mi>s</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>·</mo><mfrac><mi>π</mi><mn>3</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>10</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac><mi>π</mi></math>.

question.question: A plane triangle has angles <math><mn>40</mn><mo>°</mo></math>, <math><mn>60</mn><mo>°</mo></math>, and <math><mn>80</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. If a spherical triangle has the same three angle measures, which statement must be true?
choices: <math><mtext>The spherical triangle is impossible because triangle angles cannot sum to </mtext><mn>180</mn><mo>°</mo><mtext> on a sphere.</mtext></math>
<math><mtext>The spherical triangle has spherical excess </mtext><mn>0</mn><mo>°</mo><mtext> and corresponds to a “very small” triangle on the sphere.</mtext></math>
<math><mtext>The spherical triangle must have spherical excess </mtext><mn>180</mn><mo>°</mo><mtext>.</mtext></math>
<math><mtext>The spherical triangle must have angle sum less than </mtext><mn>180</mn><mo>°</mo><mtext>.</mtext></math>
question.explanation: Spherical excess is <math><mi>E</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>180</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. Here the sum is <math><mn>180</mn><mo>°</mo></math>, so <math><mi>E</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. This corresponds to a limiting case where the triangle is extremely small and locally behaves like Euclidean geometry.

question.question: Which statement correctly compares similarity in Euclidean and spherical geometry?
choices: <math><mtext>In Euclidean geometry, all similar triangles are congruent.</mtext></math>
<math><mtext>In spherical geometry, similar triangles can have different sizes without being congruent.</mtext></math>
<math><mtext>In spherical geometry, all similar triangles are congruent.</mtext></math>
<math><mtext>In Euclidean geometry, triangle angle sum is greater than </mtext><mn>180</mn><mo>°</mo></math>
question.explanation: On a sphere, triangles with the same angles are forced to have the same size because curvature fixes side lengths relative to angles, so similarity implies congruence.

question.question: On Earth, consider a spherical triangle formed by two meridians that are <math><mn>90</mn><mo>°</mo></math> apart and the equator, meeting at the North Pole. If each of the three angles of this triangle is <math><mn>90</mn><mo>°</mo></math>, what is the spherical excess <math><mi>E</mi></math>?
question.explanation: Angle sum is <math><mn>90</mn><mo>°</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>90</mn><mo>°</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>90</mn><mo>°</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>270</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. So <math><mi>E</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>270</mn><mo>°</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>180</mn><mo>°</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>90</mn><mo>°</mo></math>.

question.question: A sphere has radius <math><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>6371</mn></math> km. Two locations have a central angle of <math><mi>Δσ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.50</mn></math> radians between them. Using <math><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>r</mi><mi>Δσ</mi></math>, what is the approximate surface distance <math><mi>d</mi></math>?
question.explanation: Compute <math><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>r</mi><mi>Δσ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>6371</mn><mo>·</mo><mn>0.50</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>3185.5</mn></math> km.

question.question: A student claims: “Since great circles look curved on many flat maps, the shortest route between two cities is always a straight line on the map.” Which response best explains the mistake?
choices: <math><mtext>The map is always perfectly accurate, so the student is correct.</mtext></math>
<math><mtext>On Earth, shortest paths follow great-circle arcs, but map projections can distort shape so a great-circle route may not appear straight on the map.</mtext></math>
<math><mtext>Shortest paths on Earth must always follow constant latitude lines.</mtext></math>
<math><mtext>Great circles never intersect, so routes cannot follow them.</mtext></math>
question.explanation: Navigation distance on Earth is measured along the curved surface, where geodesics are great-circle arcs. Map projections flatten the sphere and distort distances/shapes, so the shortest surface path may appear curved on a flat map.

question.question: In hyperbolic geometry, how does the angle sum of a triangle compare to <math><mn>180</mn><mo>°</mo></math>?
question.explanation: A key qualitative feature of hyperbolic geometry is negative curvature, which causes triangle angle sums to be less than <math><mn>180</mn><mo>°</mo></math>.

question.question: A convex polyhedron has <math><mi>V</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></math> vertices and <math><mi>E</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>12</mn></math> edges. Using Euler’s formula <math><mi>V</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>E</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>F</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></math>, how many faces <math><mi>F</mi></math> does it have?
question.explanation: Euler’s formula gives <math><mi>F</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>V</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>E</mi></math>. Substituting <math><mi>V</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></math> and <math><mi>E</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>12</mn></math> yields <math><mi>F</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>12</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn></math>.

question.question: Which solid is not a polyhedron because it has a curved surface?
question.explanation: A polyhedron is made only of flat polygonal faces. A cylinder has a curved lateral surface, so it is not a polyhedron.

question.question: A cylinder has radius <math><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></math> cm and height <math><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></math> cm. Its net includes a rectangle for the lateral surface. What are the rectangle’s dimensions?
question.explanation: The rectangle’s height equals the cylinder height <math><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></math>. The rectangle’s length equals the circumference <math><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi><mo>·</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn><mi>π</mi></math>. So the dimensions are <math><mn>6</mn><mi>π</mi></math> cm by <math><mn>8</mn></math> cm.

question.question: A right circular cylinder has radius <math><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></math> cm and height <math><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></math> cm. A plane cuts the cylinder perpendicular to the base and passes through the axis. What is the cross-section shape and its area?
question.explanation: A perpendicular cut through the axis forms a rectangle with height <math><mn>10</mn></math> and width equal to the diameter <math><mn>2</mn><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></math>. Area <math><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>·</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>100</mn></math>.

question.question: A sphere has radius <math><mi>R</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>13</mn></math> cm. A plane cuts the sphere at a distance <math><mn>5</mn></math> cm from the center, forming a circular cross-section. What is the radius of the cross-section circle?
question.explanation: The radius <math><mi>r</mi></math> of the cross-section satisfies <math><msup><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>−</mo><msup><mn>5</mn><mn>2</mn></msup></math>. So <math><msup><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>169</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>25</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>144</mn></math>, giving <math><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mn>144</mn></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mn>12</mn></math>.

question.question: A square pyramid has base side length <math><mn>18</mn></math> and height <math><mn>12</mn></math>. A plane parallel to the base cuts the pyramid at a point <math><mn>4</mn></math> units above the base. What is the side length of the square cross-section?
question.explanation: The cut is parallel to the base, so the cross-section is similar to the base. The distance from the apex to the base is <math><mn>12</mn></math>, and the distance from the apex to the cut is <math><mn>12</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></math>. Scale factor <math><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>8</mn><mn>12</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>2</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac></math>, so side length <math><mo>=</mo><mn>18</mn><mo>·</mo><mfrac><mn>2</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>12</mn></math>.

question.question: A rectangular prism has side lengths <math><mn>6</mn></math>, <math><mn>8</mn></math>, and <math><mn>24</mn></math>. What is the length of the space diagonal (the segment connecting opposite vertices)?
question.explanation: Use the 3D Pythagorean theorem: <math><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><msqrt><msup><mn>6</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mn>8</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mn>24</mn><mn>2</mn></msup></msqrt></math> = <math><msqrt><mn>36</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>64</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>576</mn></msqrt></math> = <math><msqrt><mn>676</mn></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mn>26</mn></math>.

question.question: A triangular prism is a convex polyhedron. How many faces, edges, and vertices does a triangular prism have?
question.explanation: A triangular prism has 2 triangular bases and 3 rectangular lateral faces for a total of <math><mn>5</mn></math> faces. Each triangular base has 3 edges (6 total) plus 3 connecting edges, giving <math><mn>9</mn></math> edges, and it has 6 vertices.

question.question: A convex polyhedron has <math><mi>V</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></math> vertices and <math><mi>F</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>7</mn></math> faces. How many edges <math><mi>E</mi></math> does it have?
question.explanation: From <math><mi>V</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>E</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>F</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></math>, solve for <math><mi>E</mi></math>: <math><mi>E</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>V</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>F</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></math>. Thus <math><mi>E</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>15</mn></math>.

question.question: A plane cuts a cone parallel to the circular base. What is the shape of the cross-section?
question.explanation: A slice parallel to the base of a cone produces a smaller circle because the intersection is a constant distance from the apex in a direction perpendicular to the axis.

question.question: A right rectangular prism is cut by a plane that intersects the top and bottom faces in diagonal segments, creating a “slanted” slice through the solid. What 2D shape is a typical cross-section of this diagonal cut?
question.explanation: A diagonal plane through a prism often meets opposite lateral faces in parallel segments, producing a parallelogram cross-section (a rectangle only in special right-angle orientations).

question.question: A rectangle is rotated around one of its sides as an axis, forming a solid of revolution. Which solid is formed?
question.explanation: Rotating a rectangle around a side sweeps out a cylinder: the axis side becomes the height, and the opposite side’s distance to the axis becomes the radius.

question.question: A hemisphere of radius <math><mn>4</mn></math> cm is attached to the top of a right circular cylinder with the same radius and height <math><mn>10</mn></math> cm. What is the exact total volume of the combined solid?
question.explanation: Cylinder volume: <math><mi>V</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>π</mi><msup><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>π</mi><mo>·</mo><msup><mn>4</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>·</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>160</mn><mi>π</mi></math>. Hemisphere volume is half a sphere: <math><mi>V</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>·</mo><mfrac><mn>4</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac><mi>π</mi><msup><mn>4</mn><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>2</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac><mi>π</mi><mo>·</mo><mn>64</mn><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>128</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac><mi>π</mi></math>. Total <math><mo>=</mo><mn>160</mn><mi>π</mi><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mn>128</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac><mi>π</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>480</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac><mi>π</mi><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mn>128</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac><mi>π</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>608</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac><mi>π</mi></math> cm<math><msup><mn>3</mn><mn> </mn></msup></math>.

question.question: A cube is cut by a plane that passes through the midpoints of six edges (one midpoint on each face), producing a symmetric cross-section. What is the resulting 2D cross-section shape?
question.explanation: That slicing plane intersects six faces in equal-length segments arranged symmetrically, creating a regular hexagon cross-section.

question.question: In 3D coordinate space, points are <math><mi>A</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>)</mo></math> and <math><mi>B</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>)</mo></math>. What is the distance <math><mi>AB</mi></math>?
question.explanation: Use the 3D distance formula: <math><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><msqrt><msup><mo>(</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mo>(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mo>(</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>)</mo><mn>2</mn></msup></msqrt></math> = <math><msqrt><mn>16</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>9</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>16</mn></msqrt><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mn>41</mn></msqrt></math>.

question.question: In circle <math><mi>O</mi></math>, the central angle <math><mo>∠</mo><mi>AOB</mi></math> measures <math><mn>65</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. What is the measure of the minor arc <math><mover><mi>AB</mi><mo>⌢</mo></mover></math>?
question.explanation: A central angle and its intercepted arc (in degrees) have equal measure. So <math><mi>m</mi><mover><mi>AB</mi><mo>⌢</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>∠</mo><mi>AOB</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>65</mn><mo>°</mo></math>.

question.question: A circle has radius <math><mn>9</mn></math> cm. Which expression equals the circumference of the circle?
question.explanation: Circumference is <math><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi><mi>r</mi></math>. With <math><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>9</mn></math>, <math><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>9</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>18</mn><mi>π</mi></math>.

question.question: In a circle, the measure of a major arc is <math><mn>230</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. What is the measure of the corresponding minor arc with the same endpoints?
question.explanation: The measures of a major arc and its corresponding minor arc add to <math><mn>360</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. So the minor arc is <math><mn>360</mn><mo>°</mo><mo>-</mo><mn>230</mn><mo>°</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>130</mn><mo>°</mo></math>.

question.question: In circle <math><mi>O</mi></math>, chord <math><mi>AB</mi></math> is congruent to chord <math><mi>CD</mi></math>. If the measure of arc <math><mover><mi>AB</mi><mo>⌢</mo></mover></math> is <math><mn>98</mn><mo>°</mo></math>, what is the measure of arc <math><mover><mi>CD</mi><mo>⌢</mo></mover></math>?
question.explanation: Equal chords in the same circle intercept equal arcs. Since <math><mi>AB</mi><mo>≅</mo><mi>CD</mi></math>, we have <math><mi>m</mi><mover><mi>CD</mi><mo>⌢</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mi>m</mi><mover><mi>AB</mi><mo>⌢</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mn>98</mn><mo>°</mo></math>.

question.question: A circle has radius <math><mn>12</mn></math> cm. The measure of minor arc <math><mover><mi>PQ</mi><mo>⌢</mo></mover></math> is <math><mn>75</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. What is the length of arc <math><mover><mi>PQ</mi><mo>⌢</mo></mover></math>?
question.explanation: Use <math><mi>s</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>m</mi><mn>360</mn></mfrac><mo>·</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi><mi>r</mi></math>. With <math><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>75</mn></math> and <math><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>12</mn></math>, <math><mi>s</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>75</mn><mn>360</mn></mfrac><mo>·</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>12</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>5</mn><mn>24</mn></mfrac><mo>·</mo><mn>24</mn><mi>π</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn><mi>π</mi></math>.
