Also <math><mi>AB</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn></math> and <math><mi>CD</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn></math>, and <math><mi>BC</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></math> and <math><mi>AD</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></math>. This matches a rectangle.

question.question: Find the distance between <math><mi>G</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>-2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>-5</mn><mo>)</mo></math> and <math><mi>H</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>-1</mn><mo>)</mo></math> in simplest radical form.
question.explanation: Compute <math><mi>Δx</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>-</mo><mo>(</mo><mn>-2</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn></math> and <math><mi>Δy</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>-1</mn><mo>-</mo><mo>(</mo><mn>-5</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></math>. Distance <math><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><msqrt><msup><mn>6</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mn>4</mn><mn>2</mn></msup></msqrt><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mn>36</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>16</mn></msqrt><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mn>52</mn></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><msqrt><mn>13</mn></msqrt></math>. (Thus the correct choice is <math><mn>2</mn><msqrt><mn>13</mn></msqrt></math>.)

question.question: A circle is defined as the set of all points that are <math><mn>5</mn></math> units from the center <math><mo>(</mo><mn>-3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo></math>. Which equation represents this circle?
question.explanation: A circle with center <math><mo>(</mo><mi>h</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>)</mo></math> and radius <math><mi>r</mi></math> has equation <math><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>-</mo><mi>h</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>-</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math>. Here <math><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>-3</mn></math>, <math><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></math>, and <math><msup><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>25</mn></math>, giving <math><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>-</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>25</mn></math>.

question.question: Point <math><mi>P</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>-5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>)</mo></math> is translated <math><mn>3</mn></math> units right and <math><mn>6</mn></math> units down to point <math><mi>P'</mi></math>. What are the coordinates of <math><mi>P'</mi></math>?
question.explanation: Moving right increases <math><mi>x</mi></math> by <math><mn>3</mn></math>: <math><mn>-5</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>-2</mn></math>. Moving down decreases <math><mi>y</mi></math> by <math><mn>6</mn></math>: <math><mn>8</mn><mo>-</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></math>. So <math><mi>P'</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>-2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo></math>.

question.question: Points <math><mi>A</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>-1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>)</mo></math>, <math><mi>B</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>)</mo></math>, <math><mi>C</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>)</mo></math> form triangle <math><mi>ABC</mi></math>. Which statement is true about triangle <math><mi>ABC</mi></math>?
choices: <math><mtext>It is equilateral because all three sides are equal.</mtext></math>
<math><mtext>It is not isosceles because no two sides are equal.</mtext></math>
question.explanation: Compute lengths. <math><mi>AB</mi></math> is horizontal: <math><mi>AB</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>|</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>-</mo><mo>(</mo><mn>-1</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>|</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn></math>. For <math><mi>AC</mi></math>: <math><mi>Δx</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>-</mo><mo>(</mo><mn>-1</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></math>, <math><mi>Δy</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>-</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></math>, so <math><mi>AC</mi><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mn>3</mn><mn>^</mn><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mn>^</mn><mn>2</mn></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></math>. For <math><mi>BC</mi></math>: <math><mi>Δx</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>-</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>-3</mn></math>, <math><mi>Δy</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>-</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></math>, so <math><mi>BC</mi><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mn>9</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>16</mn></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></math>. Thus <math><mi>AC</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>BC</mi></math>, so the triangle is isosceles.

question.question: What is the slope of the line passing through the points <math><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>)</mo></math> and <math><mo>(</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>11</mn><mo>)</mo></math>?
question.explanation: Slope is <math><mfrac><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>_</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>_</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>_</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>_</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac></math>. Here <math><mfrac><mrow><mn>11</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>6</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>8</mn><mn>4</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></math>.

question.question: What is the midpoint of the segment with endpoints <math><mo>(</mo><mn>−</mn><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>)</mo></math> and <math><mo>(</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>−</mn><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></math>?
question.explanation: Midpoint is <math><mo>(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>_</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>_</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>_</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>_</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>)</mo></math>. So <math><mfrac><mrow><mn>−</mn><mn>4</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></math> and <math><mfrac><mrow><mn>7</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>−</mn><mn>1</mn></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></math>.

question.question: What is the slope of the line through the points <math><mo>(</mo><mn>−</mn><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>)</mo></math> and <math><mo>(</mo><mn>−</mn><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>−</mn><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo></math>?
question.explanation: Both points have the same <math><mi>x</mi></math>-coordinate, so the line is vertical. A vertical line has an undefined slope.

question.question: A line has slope <math><mfrac><mn>3</mn><mn>4</mn></mfrac></math>. Which slope would guarantee a line is parallel to it?
question.explanation: Parallel lines have the same slope. So the slope must be <math><mfrac><mn>3</mn><mn>4</mn></mfrac></math>.

question.question: Line <math><mi>AB</mi></math> passes through <math><mi>A</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo></math> and <math><mi>B</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>)</mo></math>. Line <math><mi>CD</mi></math> passes through <math><mi>C</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>−</mn><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>)</mo></math> and <math><mi>D</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>)</mo></math>. Are the lines parallel?
choices: <math><mtext>Yes, because the slopes are negative reciprocals</mtext></math>
question.explanation: Slope <math><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>6</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>4</mn><mn>4</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>. Also <math><mfrac><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>−</mn><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>4</mn><mn>4</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>. Same slope means parallel.

question.question: A line has slope <math><mn>−</mn><mn>2</mn></math> and passes through the point <math><mo>(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></math>. What is the equation of the line in slope-intercept form?
question.explanation: Use <math><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>m</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></math> with <math><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>−</mn><mn>2</mn></math>. Substitute the point: <math><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>−</mn><mn>2</mn><mo>(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></math> so <math><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>−</mn><mn>6</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></math>, giving <math><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>7</mn></math>.

question.question: Which equation is in point-slope form for the line with slope <math><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac></math> passing through <math><mo>(</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>−</mn><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo></math>?
question.explanation: Point-slope form is <math><mi>y</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>_</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>_</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></math>. With point <math><mo>(</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>−</mn><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo></math>, this becomes <math><mi>y</mi><mo>−</mo><mo>(</mo><mn>−</mn><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>)</mo></math>, i.e., <math><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>)</mo></math>.

question.question: The line <math><mn>2</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></math> is written in standard form. What is the slope of this line?
question.explanation: Solve for <math><mi>y</mi></math>: <math><mn>2</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>10</mn></math>, so <math><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn></math>. The slope is <math><mn>2</mn></math>.

question.question: A line has slope <math><mn>5</mn></math>. What is the slope of any line perpendicular to it?
question.explanation: Perpendicular slopes are negative reciprocals. The negative reciprocal of <math><mn>5</mn></math> is <math><mn>−</mn><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>5</mn></mfrac></math>.

question.question: Are the lines <math><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>−</mn><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn></math> and <math><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>7</mn></math> perpendicular?
question.explanation: First line has slope <math><mn>−</mn><mn>3</mn></math>. Rewrite <math><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>7</mn></math> as <math><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>−</mn><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>7</mn></math>, which also has slope <math><mn>−</mn><mn>3</mn></math>. Equal slopes means the lines are parallel, not perpendicular.

question.question: Point <math><mi>M</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>−</mn><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></math> is the midpoint of segment <math><mover><mi>AB</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover></math>. If <math><mi>A</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>−</mn><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>)</mo></math>, what are the coordinates of <math><mi>B</mi></math>?
question.explanation: Use midpoint formula: <math><mn>2</mn><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>−</mn><mn>4</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>_</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac></math> so <math><mi>x</mi><mo>_</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></math>. Also <math><mn>−</mn><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>_</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac></math> so <math><mi>y</mi><mo>_</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>−</mn><mn>7</mn></math>. Thus <math><mi>B</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>−</mn><mn>7</mn><mo>)</mo></math>.

question.question: A taxi charges <math><mn>2.50</mn></math> dollars as a starting fee and <math><mn>0.70</mn></math> dollars per mile. If the cost is modeled by points <math><mo>(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2.50</mn><mo>)</mo></math> and <math><mo>(</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>6.00</mn><mo>)</mo></math>, what is the slope of the cost line, and what does it represent?
question.explanation: Slope is <math><mfrac><mrow><mn>6.00</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>2.50</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>3.50</mn><mn>5</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>0.70</mn></math>. It represents the rate of change in cost per mile (dollars per mile).

question.question: Consider the points <math><mi>A</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>)</mo></math>, <math><mi>B</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>)</mo></math>, and <math><mi>C</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>)</mo></math>. Which statement is true about <math><mi>△ABC</mi></math>?
choices: <math><mtext>The triangle is right because one side is horizontal and another is vertical.</mtext></math>
<math><mtext>The triangle is equilateral because all sides have the same slope.</mtext></math>
<math><mtext>The triangle is obtuse because all slopes are negative.</mtext></math>
<math><mtext>The triangle cannot be classified using slopes.</mtext></math>
question.explanation: Segment <math><mover><mi>AB</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover></math> is horizontal (same <math><mi>y</mi></math>), and <math><mover><mi>BC</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover></math> is vertical (same <math><mi>x</mi></math>). Horizontal and vertical lines are perpendicular, so the triangle is right.

question.question: Find the equation of the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining <math><mo>(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo></math> and <math><mo>(</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>)</mo></math> in slope-intercept form.
question.explanation: Midpoint is <math><mo>(</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>)</mo></math>. Segment slope is <math><mfrac><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>6</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>, so perpendicular slope is <math><mn>−</mn><mn>1</mn></math>. Line through <math><mo>(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>)</mo></math>: <math><mi>y</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>−</mn><mn>1</mn><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>)</mo></math>, so <math><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>−</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>8</mn></math>.

question.question: Find the equation of the line that is parallel to <math><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>2</mn><mn>5</mn></mfrac><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></math> and passes through <math><mo>(</mo><mn>−</mn><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>)</mo></math>.
question.explanation: Parallel lines have the same slope, so <math><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>2</mn><mn>5</mn></mfrac></math>. Use point-slope: <math><mi>y</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>2</mn><mn>5</mn></mfrac><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mo>(</mo><mn>−</mn><mn>5</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>2</mn><mn>5</mn></mfrac><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>)</mo></math>. Then <math><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>2</mn><mn>5</mn></mfrac><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>2</mn><mn>5</mn></mfrac><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>6</mn></math>.

question.question: Line <math><mi>L</mi></math> has slope <math><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></math> and y-intercept <math><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>-5</mn></math>. What is the equation of <math><mi>L</mi></math> in slope-intercept form?
question.explanation: Slope-intercept form is <math><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>m</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></math>. Substituting <math><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></math> and <math><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>-5</mn></math> gives <math><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>-</mo><mn>5</mn></math>.

question.question: Find the slope of the line passing through points <math><mi>A</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>-2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></math> and <math><mi>B</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>)</mo></math>.
question.explanation: Slope is <math><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>7</mn><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo>-</mo><mo>(</mo><mn>-2</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>6</mn><mn>6</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>.

question.question: Write the equation of the line with slope <math><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>-2</mn></math> that passes through the point <math><mo>(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>)</mo></math> in point-slope form.
question.explanation: Point-slope form is <math><mi>y</mi><mo>-</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>-</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>)</mo></math>. With point <math><mo>(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>)</mo></math> and slope <math><mn>-2</mn></math>, the equation is <math><mi>y</mi><mo>-</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>-2</mn><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>-</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>)</mo></math>.

question.question: Convert the line equation <math><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mi>x</mi><mo>-</mo><mn>3</mn></math> into standard form <math><mi>A</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>B</mi><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi></math> with integer coefficients.
question.explanation: Start with <math><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mi>x</mi><mo>-</mo><mn>3</mn></math>. Multiply by <math><mn>2</mn></math>: <math><mn>2</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>-</mo><mn>6</mn></math>. Rearrange to standard form: <math><mi>x</mi><mo>-</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn></math>.

question.question: Line <math><mi>L</mi></math> passes through points <math><mo>(</mo><mn>-1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo></math> and <math><mo>(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>-6</mn><mo>)</mo></math>. What is the equation of <math><mi>L</mi></math> in slope-intercept form?
question.explanation: Slope <math><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>-6</mn><mo>-</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>-</mo><mo>(</mo><mn>-1</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>-8</mn><mn>4</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>-2</mn></math>. Use point <math><mo>(</mo><mn>-1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo></math>: <math><mi>y</mi><mo>-</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>-2</mn><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></math> ⇒ <math><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>-2</mn><mi>x</mi></math>.

question.question: Which line is parallel to <math><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></math>?
question.explanation: Parallel lines have the same slope. The given line has slope <math><mn>4</mn></math>. The only choice with slope <math><mn>4</mn></math> is <math><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>7</mn></math>.

question.question: Which line is perpendicular to <math><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>2</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn></math>?
question.explanation: Perpendicular slopes satisfy <math><mi>m</mi><sub>1</sub><mo>·</mo><mi>m</mi><sub>2</sub><mo>=</mo><mn>-1</mn></math>. The given slope is <math><mfrac><mn>2</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac></math>, so the perpendicular slope is <math><mn>-</mn><mfrac><mn>3</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></math>. Choice C has that slope.

question.question: A circle has center <math><mo>(</mo><mn>-3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>)</mo></math> and radius <math><mn>5</mn></math>. Which equation represents this circle?
question.explanation: Circle form is <math><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>-</mo><mi>h</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>-</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math>. With <math><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>-3</mn></math> and <math><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></math>, we get <math><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>-</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>25</mn></math>.

question.question: Convert the circle equation <math><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>6</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>12</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math> to center-radius form and identify the center.
question.explanation: Group terms: <math><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>6</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>12</mn></math>. Complete squares: <math><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>25</mn></math>. Thus the center is <math><mo>(</mo><mn>−3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo></math>.

question.question: Which equation is in standard form <math><mi>A</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>B</mi><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi></math>?
question.explanation: Standard form for a line is <math><mi>A</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>B</mi><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi></math> with integer coefficients. Only <math><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>-</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></math> matches that format.

question.question: A line passes through the points <math><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>-1</mn><mo>)</mo></math> and <math><mo>(</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>)</mo></math>. What is the equation of the line in standard form?
question.explanation: Slope is <math><mfrac><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo>-</mo><mo>(</mo><mn>-1</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo>-</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>6</mn><mn>6</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>. So <math><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></math>. Substitute <math><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>-1</mn><mo>)</mo></math>: <math><mn>-1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></math> so <math><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>-3</mn></math>. Thus <math><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>-</mo><mn>3</mn></math>, which converts to standard form <math><mi>x</mi><mo>-</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></math>.

question.question: Which equation represents a parabola (not a circle, ellipse, or hyperbola)?
question.explanation: A parabola has exactly one squared variable. The equation <math><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn><mi>x</mi></math> has only one squared term, so it represents a parabola.

question.question: Which equation represents an ellipse?
question.explanation: An ellipse has both squared terms positive but with different denominators in standard form, like <math><mfrac><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><msup><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mfrac><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><msup><mi>b</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math> where <math><mi>a</mi><mo>≠</mo><mi>b</mi></math>. Choice B matches this structure.

question.question: A circle has equation <math><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>49</mn></math>. What are the center and radius?
question.explanation: In <math><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>h</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math>, the center is <math><mo>(</mo><mi>h</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>)</mo></math>. Here <math><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></math> and <math><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>−3</mn></math> because the term is <math><mo>(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>)</mo></math>. Also <math><msup><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>49</mn></math>, so <math><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>7</mn></math>.

question.question: Find the x-intercept of the line <math><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></math>.
question.explanation: The x-intercept occurs when <math><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>. Substitute into <math><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>12</mn></math>: <math><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>12</mn></math> so <math><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></math>. The x-intercept is <math><mo>(</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>)</mo></math>.

question.question: In <math><mo>△</mo><mi>ABC</mi></math>, the angle measures are <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>55</mn><mo>°</mo></math> and <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>65</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. What is <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>C</mi></math>?
question.explanation: By the Triangle Sum Theorem, <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>+</mo><mo>m∠</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>+</mo><mo>m∠</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>180</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. So <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>180</mn><mo>°</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>55</mn><mo>°</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>65</mn><mo>°</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>60</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. (Correct choice is B.)

question.question: Triangle <math><mo>△</mo><mi>DEF</mi></math> has side lengths <math><mover><mi>DE</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mn>7</mn></math>, <math><mover><mi>EF</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mn>7</mn></math>, and <math><mover><mi>DF</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></math>. How should the triangle be classified by sides?
question.explanation: An isosceles triangle has exactly two congruent sides. Since <math><mover><mi>DE</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mover><mi>EF</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover></math>, the triangle is isosceles.

question.question: In a triangle, one angle measures <math><mn>90</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. How is the triangle classified by angles?
question.explanation: A right triangle is defined as a triangle with one right angle, meaning an angle of <math><mn>90</mn><mo>°</mo></math>.

question.question: In <math><mo>△</mo><mi>ABC</mi></math>, <math><mover><mi>AB</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover><mo>≅</mo><mover><mi>AC</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover></math> and <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>42</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. What is <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>C</mi></math>?
question.explanation: If <math><mover><mi>AB</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover><mo>≅</mo><mover><mi>AC</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover></math>, then the base angles opposite those sides are congruent, so <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>m∠</mo><mi>C</mi></math>. Therefore <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>42</mn><mo>°</mo></math>.

question.question: In <math><mo>△</mo><mi>XYZ</mi></math>, <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>38</mn><mo>°</mo></math> and <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>79</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. An exterior angle is formed at vertex <math><mi>Z</mi></math> by extending <math><mover><mi>YZ</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover></math>. What is the measure of that exterior angle?
question.explanation: By the Exterior Angle Theorem, the exterior angle at <math><mi>Z</mi></math> equals the sum of the two remote interior angles: <math><mn>38</mn><mo>°</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>79</mn><mo>°</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>117</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. (Correct choice is A.)

question.question: Which set of side lengths can form a triangle?
question.explanation: By the Triangle Inequality Theorem, the sum of any two sides must be greater than the third. For <math><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>12</mn></math>: <math><mn>6</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>13</mn><mo>></mo><mn>12</mn></math>, and the other sums also exceed the remaining side, so it forms a triangle. The other options fail because two sides sum to the third or less.

question.question: Two triangles have side lengths <math><mn>5</mn></math>, <math><mn>7</mn></math>, <math><mn>9</mn></math> and <math><mn>5</mn></math>, <math><mn>7</mn></math>, <math><mn>9</mn></math>. Which congruence postulate proves the triangles are congruent?
question.explanation: If all three corresponding sides are congruent, then the triangles are congruent by <math><mtext>SSS</mtext></math>.

question.question: In triangles <math><mo>△</mo><mi>ABC</mi></math> and <math><mo>△</mo><mi>DEF</mi></math>, suppose <math><mover><mi>AB</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover><mo>≅</mo><mover><mi>DE</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover></math>, <math><mover><mi>AC</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover><mo>≅</mo><mover><mi>DF</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover></math>, and <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>m∠</mo><mi>D</mi></math>. Which congruence postulate applies?
question.explanation: Two sides and the included angle are congruent (<math><mover><mi>AB</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover></math> with <math><mover><mi>AC</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover></math> include <math><mo>∠</mo><mi>A</mi></math>), so the triangles are congruent by <math><mtext>SAS</mtext></math>.

question.question: Triangles <math><mo>△</mo><mi>PQR</mi></math> and <math><mo>△</mo><mi>STU</mi></math> are right triangles with right angles at <math><mi>Q</mi></math> and <math><mi>T</mi></math>. If <math><mover><mi>PR</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover><mo>≅</mo><mover><mi>SU</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover></math> and <math><mover><mi>PQ</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover><mo>≅</mo><mover><mi>ST</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover></math>, which congruence theorem proves the triangles are congruent?
question.explanation: In right triangles, if the hypotenuse and one leg are congruent, then the triangles are congruent by <math><mtext>HL</mtext></math>. question.question: In <math><mo>△</mo><mi>ABC</mi></math>, <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>10</mn></math>, <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></math>, and <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>75</mn></math>. question.explanation: Triangle sum: <math><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>+</mo><mo>(</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>75</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>180</mn></math>. question.question: In <math><mo>△</mo><mi>ABC</mi></math>, an exterior angle at <math><mi>C</mi></math> has measure <math><mn>150</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. If <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>10</mn></math> and <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>20</mn></math>, what is <math><mi>t</mi></math>?
question.explanation: By the Exterior Angle Theorem, <math><mn>150</mn><mo>=</mo><mo>m∠</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>+</mo><mo>m∠</mo><mi>B</mi></math>. So <math><mn>150</mn><mo>=</mo><mo>(</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>+</mo><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>20</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>30</mn></math>. question.question: Triangles <math><mo>△</mo><mi>ABC</mi></math> and <math><mo>△</mo><mi>DEF</mi></math> have <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>m∠</mo><mi>D</mi></math>, <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>m∠</mo><mi>E</mi></math>, and <math><mover><mi>AC</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover><mo>≅</mo><mover><mi>DF</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover></math>. question.question: In <math><mo>△</mo><mi>ABC</mi></math>, <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>35</mn><mo>°</mo></math> and <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>35</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. Which statement must be true?
question.explanation: If two angles of a triangle are congruent, then the sides opposite them are congruent (converse of the Base Angles Theorem). question.question: In <math><mo>△</mo><mi>ABC</mi></math>, the side lengths satisfy <math><mover><mi>AB</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mn>9</mn></math>, <math><mover><mi>BC</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mn>12</mn></math>, and <math><mover><mi>AC</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi></math>. question.question: Which set of side lengths can form a triangle by the Triangle Inequality Theorem?
question.explanation: A triangle is possible only if the sum of any two sides is greater than the third. For <math><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>10</mn></math>: <math><mn>5</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>11</mn><mo>></mo><mn>10</mn></math>, <math><mn>5</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>></mo><mn>6</mn></math>, and <math><mn>6</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>></mo><mn>5</mn></math>. The other options fail because two sides sum to the third or less.

question.question: Two sides of a triangle have lengths <math><mn>9</mn></math> and <math><mn>14</mn></math>. Which inequality describes all possible values of the third side <math><mi>x</mi></math>?
question.explanation: Use the range form of triangle inequality: <math><mo>|</mo><mn>14</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>9</mn><mo>|</mo><mo><</mo><mi>x</mi><mo><</mo><mn>14</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>9</mn></math>. This gives <math><mn>5</mn><mo><</mo><mi>x</mi><mo><</mo><mn>23</mn></math> (strict inequalities).

question.question: Two sides of a triangle are <math><mn>6</mn></math> and <math><mn>11</mn></math>. How many integer values can the third side <math><mi>x</mi></math> have?
question.explanation: Triangle inequality gives <math><mo>|</mo><mn>11</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>|</mo><mo><</mo><mi>x</mi><mo><</mo><mn>11</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>6</mn></math>, so <math><mn>5</mn><mo><</mo><mi>x</mi><mo><</mo><mn>17</mn></math>. Integer values are <math><mn>6</mn></math> through <math><mn>16</mn></math>, which is <math><mn>11</mn></math> integers.

question.question: In <math><mo>△</mo><mi>ABC</mi></math>, if <math><mover><mi>AB</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover></math> is the longest side, which angle must be the largest?
question.explanation: The longest side lies opposite the largest angle. Side <math><mover><mi>AB</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover></math> is opposite <math><mo>∠</mo><mi>C</mi></math>, so <math><mo>∠</mo><mi>C</mi></math> is the largest.

question.question: In <math><mo>△</mo><mi>PQR</mi></math>, the angles satisfy <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>></mo><mo>m∠</mo><mi>Q</mi></math>. Which statement must be true about the opposite sides?
question.explanation: A larger angle has a longer opposite side. <math><mo>∠</mo><mi>P</mi></math> is opposite <math><mover><mi>QR</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover></math> and <math><mo>∠</mo><mi>Q</mi></math> is opposite <math><mover><mi>PR</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover></math>. So <math><mover><mi>QR</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover><mo>></mo><mover><mi>PR</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover></math>.

question.question: Triangles <math><mo>△</mo><mi>ABC</mi></math> and <math><mo>△</mo><mi>DEF</mi></math> satisfy <math><mover><mi>AB</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover><mo>≅</mo><mover><mi>DE</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover></math> and <math><mover><mi>AC</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover><mo>≅</mo><mover><mi>DF</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover></math>. If <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>></mo><mo>m∠</mo><mi>D</mi></math>, what can you conclude about <math><mover><mi>BC</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover></math> and <math><mover><mi>EF</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover></math>?
question.explanation: By the Hinge Theorem (SAS Inequality), if two pairs of corresponding sides are congruent, then the triangle with the larger included angle has the longer third side. Since <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>></mo><mo>m∠</mo><mi>D</mi></math>, we conclude <math><mover><mi>BC</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover><mo>></mo><mover><mi>EF</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover></math>.

question.question: Triangles <math><mo>△</mo><mi>JKL</mi></math> and <math><mo>△</mo><mi>MNP</mi></math> satisfy <math><mover><mi>JK</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover><mo>≅</mo><mover><mi>MN</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover></math> and <math><mover><mi>JL</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover><mo>≅</mo><mover><mi>MP</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover></math>. question.explanation: By the Converse Hinge Theorem (SSS Inequality), if two pairs of sides are congruent and one triangle has a longer third side, then it has a larger included angle. Since <math><mover><mi>KL</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover><mo>></mo><mover><mi>NP</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover></math>, the included angle <math><mo>∠</mo><mi>J</mi></math> is larger than <math><mo>∠</mo><mi>M</mi></math>.

question.question: In <math><mo>△</mo><mi>ABC</mi></math>, an exterior angle at <math><mi>C</mi></math> measures <math><mn>125</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. Which statement must be true?

question.question: A triangle has side lengths <math><mn>8</mn></math>, <math><mn>12</mn></math>, and <math><mn>15</mn></math>. Order the angles from smallest to largest.

question.question: In <math><mo>△</mo><mi>ABC</mi></math>, <math><mover><mi>AD</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover></math> is a median to <math><mover><mi>BC</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover></math>. question.question: In <math><mo>△</mo><mi>ABC</mi></math>, points <math><mi>D</mi></math> and <math><mi>E</mi></math> are the midpoints of <math><mover><mi>AB</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover></math> and <math><mover><mi>AC</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover></math>, respectively. question.question: Points <math><mi>P</mi></math> and <math><mi>Q</mi></math> are on a perpendicular bisector of segment <math><mover><mi>AB</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover></math>. Which statement must be true?

question.question: In <math><mo>△</mo><mi>ABC</mi></math>, <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>30</mn><mo>°</mo></math>, <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>70</mn><mo>°</mo></math>, and <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>80</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. Which side is the longest?

question.question: A triangle has side lengths <math><mn>10</mn></math>, <math><mn>13</mn></math>, and <math><mi>x</mi></math>. If <math><mi>x</mi></math> is an integer, what is the greatest possible value of <math><mi>x</mi></math>?

question.question: In triangles <math><mi>ABC</mi></math> and <math><mi>DEF</mi></math>, suppose <math><mo>∠</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>≅</mo><mo>∠</mo><mi>D</mi></math> and <math><mo>∠</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>≅</mo><mo>∠</mo><mi>E</mi></math>. question.question: Triangles <math><mo>△</mo><mi>PQR</mi></math> and <math><mo>△</mo><mi>STU</mi></math> are similar with correspondence <math><mi>P</mi><mo>↔</mo><mi>S</mi></math>, <math><mi>Q</mi><mo>↔</mo><mi>T</mi></math>, <math><mi>R</mi><mo>↔</mo><mi>U</mi></math>. question.question: Triangles <math><mo>△</mo><mi>ABC</mi></math> and <math><mo>△</mo><mi>DEF</mi></math> are similar. question.question: In a <math><mn>45</mn><mo>°</mo></math>–<math><mn>45</mn><mo>°</mo></math>–<math><mn>90</mn><mo>°</mo></math> triangle, each leg is <math><mn>7</mn></math>. What is the hypotenuse?

question.question: In a <math><mn>30</mn><mo>°</mo></math>–<math><mn>60</mn><mo>°</mo></math>–<math><mn>90</mn><mo>°</mo></math> triangle, the short leg is <math><mn>4</mn></math>. What is the long leg?
question.explanation: For a <math><mn>30</mn><mo>°</mo></math>–<math><mn>60</mn><mo>°</mo></math>–<math><mn>90</mn><mo>°</mo></math> triangle, side ratios are <math><mi>x</mi><mo>:</mo><mi>x</mi><msqrt><mn>3</mn></msqrt><mo>:</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi></math>. If the short leg <math><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></math>, then the long leg is <math><mn>4</mn><msqrt><mn>3</mn></msqrt></math>.

question.question: In right triangle <math><mi>ABC</mi></math> with right angle at <math><mi>C</mi></math>, suppose <math><mi>AC</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>9</mn></math> and <math><mi>AB</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>15</mn></math>. What is <math><mi>sin</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mo>∠</mo><mi>B</mi></math>?
question.explanation: With right angle at <math><mi>C</mi></math>, the hypotenuse is <math><mi>AB</mi></math>. question.question: In right triangle <math><mi>RST</mi></math> with right angle at <math><mi>S</mi></math>, suppose the leg opposite <math><mo>∠</mo><mi>R</mi></math> is <math><mn>6</mn></math> and the leg adjacent to <math><mo>∠</mo><mi>R</mi></math> is <math><mn>8</mn></math>. What is <math><mi>tan</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mo>∠</mo><mi>R</mi></math>?
question.explanation: <math><mi>tan</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mo>∠</mo><mi>R</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mtext>opposite</mtext><mtext>adjacent</mtext></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>6</mn><mn>8</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>3</mn><mn>4</mn></mfrac></math>.

question.question: In a right triangle, an altitude is drawn to the hypotenuse, splitting the hypotenuse into segments of lengths <math><mn>9</mn></math> and <math><mn>16</mn></math>. What is the length of the altitude?
question.explanation: For a right triangle, the altitude <math><mi>h</mi></math> to the hypotenuse satisfies <math><msup><mi>h</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>p</mi><mi>q</mi></math>. Here <math><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>9</mn></math> and <math><mi>q</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>16</mn></math>, so <math><msup><mi>h</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>144</mn></math> and <math><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>12</mn></math>.

question.question: In a right triangle, the hypotenuse has length <math><mn>25</mn></math>. The altitude to the hypotenuse splits it so that the segment adjacent to leg <math><mi>a</mi></math> has length <math><mn>9</mn></math>. What is the length of leg <math><mi>a</mi></math>?
question.explanation: A leg satisfies the geometric-mean relationship <math><msup><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi><mi>p</mi></math>, where <math><mi>c</mi></math> is the hypotenuse and <math><mi>p</mi></math> is the adjacent hypotenuse segment. So <math><msup><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>25</mn><mo>·</mo><mn>9</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>225</mn></math>, giving <math><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>15</mn></math>.

question.question: In triangles <math><mo>△</mo><mi>ABC</mi></math> and <math><mo>△</mo><mi>DEF</mi></math>, suppose <math><mo>∠</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>≅</mo><mo>∠</mo><mi>D</mi></math>, <math><mi>AB</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></math>, <math><mi>AC</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></math>, <math><mi>DE</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn></math>, and <math><mi>DF</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>15</mn></math>. question.explanation: The side ratios are <math><mfrac><mi>DE</mi><mi>AB</mi></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>6</mn><mn>4</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>3</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></math> and <math><mfrac><mi>DF</mi><mi>AC</mi></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>15</mn><mn>10</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>3</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></math>. With the included angle congruent, triangles are similar by <math><mtext>SAS</mtext></math>, and the scale factor from <math><mo>△</mo><mi>ABC</mi></math> to <math><mo>△</mo><mi>DEF</mi></math> is <math><mfrac><mn>3</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></math>.

question.question: A person who is <math><mn>6</mn></math> ft tall casts a shadow that is <math><mn>8</mn></math> ft long. At the same time, a tree casts a shadow that is <math><mn>20</mn></math> ft long. Assuming the sun’s rays form similar triangles, what is the height of the tree?
question.explanation: Similar triangles give equal height-to-shadow ratios: <math><mfrac><mn>6</mn><mn>8</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>h</mi><mn>20</mn></mfrac></math>. Solve: <math><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>20</mn><mo>·</mo><mfrac><mn>6</mn><mn>8</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>20</mn><mo>·</mo><mfrac><mn>3</mn><mn>4</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>15</mn></math> ft.

The hypotenuse is <math><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>9</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>13</mn></math>.

question.question: What is the sum of the interior angles of any quadrilateral?
question.explanation: A quadrilateral has <math><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></math> sides, so its interior angle sum is <math><mo>(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo><mn>180</mn><mo>°</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>(</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo><mn>180</mn><mo>°</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>360</mn><mo>°</mo></math>.

question.question: The sum of the exterior angles of any polygon (taking one exterior angle at each vertex) is always:
choices: <math><mtext>It depends on the number of sides</mtext></math>
question.explanation: For any polygon, the sum of one exterior angle at each vertex is always <math><mn>360</mn><mo>°</mo></math>, regardless of the number of sides.

question.question: What is the sum of the interior angles of a <math><mn>9</mn></math>-gon?
question.explanation: Use the interior angle sum formula <math><mo>(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo><mn>180</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. For <math><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>9</mn></math>, the sum is <math><mo>(</mo><mn>9</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo><mn>180</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>·</mo><mn>180</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>1260</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. (So the correct choice is <math><mn>1260</mn><mo>°</mo></math>.)

question.question: A regular polygon has each exterior angle measuring <math><mn>24</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. How many sides does the polygon have?
question.explanation: In a regular polygon, each exterior angle is <math><mfrac><mn>360</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac><mo>°</mo></math>. Set <math><mfrac><mn>360</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>24</mn></math>, so <math><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>360</mn><mn>24</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>15</mn></math>. The polygon has <math><mn>15</mn></math> sides.

question.question: A regular polygon has <math><mn>12</mn></math> sides. What is the measure of each interior angle?
question.explanation: Each interior angle of a regular <math><mi>n</mi></math>-gon is <math><mfrac><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo><mn>180</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></mfrac><mo>°</mo></math>. For <math><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>12</mn></math>, <math><mfrac><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>12</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo><mn>180</mn></mrow><mn>12</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1800</mn><mn>12</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>150</mn><mo>°</mo></math>.

question.question: Which statement is always true for a parallelogram <math><mi>ABCD</mi></math>?
question.explanation: A parallelogram is defined by having both pairs of opposite sides parallel, and it also has the property that opposite sides are congruent. The other properties are only guaranteed for special parallelograms like rhombi or rectangles.

question.question: In parallelogram <math><mi>WXYZ</mi></math>, <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>W</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>68</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. What is <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>X</mi></math>?
question.explanation: Consecutive angles in a parallelogram are supplementary. Since <math><mo>∠</mo><mi>W</mi></math> and <math><mo>∠</mo><mi>X</mi></math> are consecutive, <math><mo>m∠</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>180</mn><mo>°</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>68</mn><mo>°</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>112</mn><mo>°</mo></math>.

question.question: In parallelogram <math><mi>ABCD</mi></math>, diagonals <math><mover><mi>AC</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover></math> and <math><mover><mi>BD</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover></math> intersect at <math><mi>M</mi></math>. If <math><mover><mi>AM</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mn>7</mn></math>, what is <math><mover><mi>AC</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover></math>?
question.explanation: Diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other, so <math><mover><mi>AM</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mover><mi>MC</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover></math>. Therefore <math><mover><mi>AC</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mover><mi>AM</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover><mo>+</mo><mover><mi>MC</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>14</mn></math>.

question.question: Which additional property is guaranteed for a rectangle but not for every parallelogram?
question.explanation: A rectangle is a parallelogram with four right angles, and it also has congruent diagonals. Diagonals bisect each other and opposite sides are parallel in every parallelogram, so those do not uniquely identify rectangles.

question.question: In rectangle <math><mi>ABCD</mi></math>, diagonals are drawn. If <math><mover><mi>AC</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mn>26</mn></math>, what is <math><mover><mi>BD</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover></math>?
question.explanation: Diagonals of a rectangle are congruent, so <math><mover><mi>BD</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mover><mi>AC</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mn>26</mn></math>.

question.question: Which statement is always true for a rhombus?
choices: <math><mtext>Exactly one pair of opposite sides is parallel</mtext></math>
question.explanation: A rhombus is a parallelogram with four congruent sides. Its angles do not have to be right angles (that would make it a square), and its diagonals are not always congruent.

question.question: In a rhombus <math><mi>QRST</mi></math>, diagonals <math><mover><mi>QS</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover></math> and <math><mover><mi>RT</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover></math> intersect at right angles. question.explanation: The area of a rhombus can be found using diagonals: <math><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><msub><mi>d</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><msub><mi>d</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math>. Here <math><msub><mi>d</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></math> and <math><msub><mi>d</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>24</mn></math>, so <math><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>(</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>(</mo><mn>24</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>120</mn></math>.

question.question: In an isosceles trapezoid <math><mi>ABCD</mi></math> with bases <math><mover><mi>AB</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover></math> and <math><mover><mi>CD</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover></math>, the base angles at base <math><mover><mi>AB</mi><mo>‾</mo></mover></math> are congruent. question.question: A right triangle has angles <math><mn>45</mn><mo>°</mo></math>, <math><mn>45</mn><mo>°</mo></math>, and <math><mn>90</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. If one leg is <math><mn>5</mn><msqrt><mn>2</mn></msqrt></math>, what is the length of the hypotenuse?

question.question: A rectangular flag has width <math><mn>8</mn></math> ft and height <math><mn>8</mn></math> ft, so its diagonal forms a <math><mn>45</mn><mo>°</mo></math>–<math><mn>45</mn><mo>°</mo></math>–<math><mn>90</mn><mo>°</mo></math> triangle. If the diagonal is extended to create two identical right isosceles triangles, what is the total length of the two diagonals combined?
question.explanation: One diagonal is the hypotenuse of a <math><mn>45</mn><mo>°</mo></math>–<math><mn>45</mn><mo>°</mo></math>–<math><mn>90</mn><mo>°</mo></math> triangle with leg <math><mn>8</mn></math>, so diagonal <math><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn><msqrt><mn>2</mn></msqrt></math>. Two diagonals combined: <math><mn>2</mn><mo>·</mo><mn>8</mn><msqrt><mn>2</mn></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mn>16</mn><msqrt><mn>2</mn></msqrt></math>.

question.question: A right triangle is known to be a <math><mn>30</mn><mo>°</mo></math>–<math><mn>60</mn><mo>°</mo></math>–<math><mn>90</mn><mo>°</mo></math> triangle. The perimeter is <math><mn>30</mn></math>. What is the length of the short leg in simplest form?
question.explanation: Let short leg be <math><mi>x</mi></math>. Then long leg <math><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><msqrt><mn>3</mn></msqrt></math> and hypotenuse <math><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi></math>. Perimeter: <math><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><msqrt><mn>3</mn></msqrt><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>30</mn></math> so <math><mi>x</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo><msqrt><mn>3</mn></msqrt><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>30</mn></math>. Thus <math><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>30</mn><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo><msqrt><mn>3</mn></msqrt></mfrac></math>. Multiply top and bottom by <math><mn>3</mn><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mn>3</mn></msqrt></math>: <math><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>30</mn><mo>(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mn>3</mn></msqrt><mo>)</mo></mfrac><mn>6</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>−</mo><msqrt><mn>3</mn></msqrt><mo>)</mo></math>. The option equivalent to <math><mfrac><mn>15</mn><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><msqrt><mn>3</mn></msqrt></mfrac></math> is not correct; the correct simplified exact form is <math><mn>15</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn><msqrt><mn>3</mn></msqrt></math>, which matches none of the listed options exactly.

question.question: A <math><mn>30</mn><mo>°</mo></math>–<math><mn>60</mn><mo>°</mo></math>–<math><mn>90</mn><mo>°</mo></math> triangle has hypotenuse <math><mn>20</mn></math>. What is the length of the short leg?
question.explanation: In a <math><mn>30</mn><mo>°</mo></math>–<math><mn>60</mn><mo>°</mo></math>–<math><mn>90</mn><mo>°</mo></math> triangle, the hypotenuse is twice the short leg: <math><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi></math>. With <math><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>20</mn></math>, <math><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>20</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></math>.

question.question: In right triangle <math><mi>ABC</mi></math>, the legs have lengths <math><mi>AB</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn></math> and <math><mi>BC</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></math>. What is the length of the hypotenuse <math><mi>AC</mi></math>?
question.explanation: By the Pythagorean Theorem, <math><msup><mi>AB</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>BC</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>AC</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math>. So <math><msup><mi>AC</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>6</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mn>8</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>36</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>64</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>100</mn></math>, hence <math><mi>AC</mi><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mn>100</mn></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></math>.

question.question: A right triangle has hypotenuse <math><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>13</mn></math> and one leg <math><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></math>. What is the length of the other leg <math><mi>b</mi></math>?
question.explanation: Use <math><msup><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>b</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>c</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math>. Then <math><msup><mi>b</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>13</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>−</mo><msup><mn>5</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>169</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>25</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>144</mn></math>, so <math><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mn>144</mn></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mn>12</mn></math>.

question.question: In a right triangle, the legs have lengths <math><mn>9</mn></math> and <math><mn>12</mn></math>. What is the length of the hypotenuse?
question.explanation: Compute <math><msqrt><msup><mn>9</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mn>12</mn><mn>2</mn></msup></msqrt><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mn>81</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>144</mn></msqrt><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mn>225</mn></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mn>15</mn></math>.

question.question: A right triangle has hypotenuse <math><mn>17</mn></math> and one leg <math><mn>8</mn></math>. What is the length of the other leg?
question.explanation: Let the missing leg be <math><mi>x</mi></math>. Then <math><msup><mn>8</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>17</mn><mn>2</mn></msup></math>. So <math><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>289</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>64</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>225</mn></math>, hence <math><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>15</mn></math>.

question.question: Find the distance between points <math><mi>P</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></math> and <math><mi>Q</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>)</mo></math> in the coordinate plane.
question.explanation: Compute <math><mi>Δx</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn></math> and <math><mi>Δy</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>−</mo><mo>(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></math>. Distance <math><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><msqrt><msup><mn>6</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mn>8</mn><mn>2</mn></msup></msqrt><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mn>36</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>64</mn></msqrt><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mn>100</mn></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></math>.

question.question: Find the distance between <math><mi>A</mi><mo>(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>)</mo></math> and <math><mi>B</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo></math>. Give your answer in simplest radical form.
question.explanation: Compute <math><mi>Δx</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>−</mo><mo>(</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></math> and <math><mi>Δy</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>=</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></math>. Then <math><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><msqrt><msup><mn>8</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mn>2</mn></msup></msqrt><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mn>64</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>9</mn></msqrt><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mn>73</mn></msqrt></math>.

question.question: A triangle has side lengths <math><mn>7</mn></math>, <math><mn>24</mn></math>, and <math><mn>25</mn></math>. Using the converse of the Pythagorean Theorem, how should the triangle be classified?
question.explanation: Let <math><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>25</mn></math> be the largest side. Compute <math><msup><mn>7</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mn>24</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>49</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>576</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>625</mn></math> and <math><msup><mn>25</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>625</mn></math>. Since they are equal, the triangle is right by the converse.

question.question: A triangle has side lengths <math><mn>9</mn></math>, <math><mn>10</mn></math>, and <math><mn>14</mn></math>. Using Pythagorean inequalities with <math><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>14</mn></math>, classify the triangle.
question.explanation: Compute <math><msup><mn>9</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>81</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>100</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>181</mn></math> and <math><msup><mn>14</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>196</mn></math>. Since <math><mn>181</mn><mo><</mo><mn>196</mn></math>, the triangle is obtuse.

question.question: A triangle has side lengths <math><mn>6</mn></math>, <math><mn>7</mn></math>, and <math><mn>8</mn></math>. Using Pythagorean inequalities with <math><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></math>, classify the triangle.
question.explanation: Let <math><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></math>. Then <math><msup><mn>6</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mn>7</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>36</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>49</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>85</mn></math>, while <math><msup><mn>8</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>64</mn></math>. Since <math><mn>85</mn><mo>></mo><mn>64</mn></math>, the triangle is acute.

question.question: A right triangle has both legs equal to <math><mn>10</mn></math>. What is the length of the hypotenuse in simplest radical form?
question.explanation: By the Pythagorean Theorem, <math><msup><mi>c</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>100</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>100</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>200</mn></math>. So <math><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mn>200</mn></msqrt><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mn>100</mn><mo>·</mo><mn>2</mn></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn><msqrt><mn>2</mn></msqrt></math>.

question.question: A rectangle has length <math><mn>12</mn></math> cm and width <math><mn>9</mn></math> cm. What is the length of the diagonal?
question.explanation: The diagonal is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs <math><mn>12</mn></math> and <math><mn>9</mn></math>. So <math><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><msqrt><msup><mn>12</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mn>9</mn><mn>2</mn></msup></msqrt><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mn>144</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>81</mn></msqrt><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mn>225</mn></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mn>15</mn></math>.

question.question: A square has side length <math><mn>5</mn></math> units. What is the length of the diagonal in simplest radical form?
question.explanation: The diagonal is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs <math><mn>5</mn></math> and <math><mn>5</mn></math>. Thus <math><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><msqrt><msup><mn>5</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mn>5</mn><mn>2</mn></msup></msqrt><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mn>25</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>25</mn></msqrt><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mn>50</mn></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><msqrt><mn>2</mn></msqrt></math>.

question.question: In three dimensions, find the distance between points <math><mi>A</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>)</mo></math> and <math><mi>B</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>)</mo></math>.
question.explanation: Use the 3D distance formula (Pythagorean Theorem applied twice): <math><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><msqrt><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mn>3</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mn>6</mn><mn>2</mn></msup></msqrt><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mn>4</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>9</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>36</mn></msqrt><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mn>49</mn></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mn>7</mn></math>.

question.question: A circle has center <math><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo></math> and passes through the point <math><mo>(</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>14</mn><mo>)</mo></math>. What is the radius of the circle?
question.explanation: The radius is the distance from center to the point: <math><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><msqrt><msup><mrow><mn>6</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow><mn>14</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></msqrt><mo>=</mo><msqrt><msup><mn>5</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mn>12</mn><mn>2</mn></msup></msqrt><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mn>25</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>144</mn></msqrt><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mn>169</mn></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mn>13</mn></math>.

question.question: A ramp rises <math><mn>3</mn></math> feet vertically while extending <math><mn>12</mn></math> feet horizontally. Assuming the ramp forms a right triangle with the ground, what is the length of the ramp in simplest radical form?
question.explanation: The ramp is the hypotenuse: <math><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><msqrt><msup><mn>3</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mn>12</mn><mn>2</mn></msup></msqrt><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mn>9</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>144</mn></msqrt><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mn>153</mn></msqrt></math>. Since <math><mn>153</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>9</mn><mo>·</mo><mn>17</mn></math>, we get <math><msqrt><mn>153</mn></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><msqrt><mn>17</mn></msqrt></math>.

question.question: In a right triangle, an acute angle is labeled <math><mi>θ</mi></math>. Which expression correctly defines <math><mo>cos</mo><mi>θ</mi></math>?
question.explanation: By definition (CAH in SOH–CAH–TOA), <math><mo>cos</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mtext>adjacent</mtext><mtext>hypotenuse</mtext></mfrac></math>.

question.question: In a right triangle, <math><mi>sin</mi><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.6</mn></math> for an acute angle <math><mi>θ</mi></math>. If the hypotenuse is <math><mn>25</mn></math>, what is the length of the side opposite <math><mi>θ</mi></math>?
question.explanation: Using <math><mi>sin</mi><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mtext>opposite</mtext><mtext>hypotenuse</mtext></mfrac></math>, we have <math><mn>0.6</mn><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>o</mi><mn>25</mn></mfrac></math>. So <math><mi>o</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.6</mn><mo>·</mo><mn>25</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>15</mn></math>.

question.question: A right triangle has an acute angle <math><mi>θ</mi></math> with opposite side length <math><mn>6</mn></math> and adjacent side length <math><mn>8</mn></math>. What is <math><mi>tan</mi><mi>θ</mi></math> in simplest form?
question.explanation: By definition, <math><mi>tan</mi><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mtext>opposite</mtext><mtext>adjacent</mtext></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>6</mn><mn>8</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>3</mn><mn>4</mn></mfrac></math>.

question.question: In a right triangle, an acute angle is <math><mn>60</mn><mo>°</mo></math> and the side adjacent to this angle is <math><mn>10</mn></math>. What is the hypotenuse?
question.explanation: Use cosine: <math><mi>cos</mi><mn>60</mn><mo>°</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>10</mn><mi>h</mi></mfrac></math>. Since <math><mi>cos</mi><mn>60</mn><mo>°</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></math>, we get <math><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>10</mn><mi>h</mi></mfrac></math>, so <math><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>20</mn></math>.

question.question: In a right triangle, the hypotenuse is <math><mn>18</mn></math> and an acute angle is <math><mn>30</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. What is the length of the side adjacent to the <math><mn>30</mn><mo>°</mo></math> angle? (Give an exact value.)
question.explanation: Use cosine: <math><mi>cos</mi><mn>30</mn><mo>°</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>a</mi><mn>18</mn></mfrac></math>. Since <math><mi>cos</mi><mn>30</mn><mo>°</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><msqrt><mn>3</mn></msqrt><mn>2</mn></mfrac></math>, <math><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>18</mn><mo>·</mo><mfrac><msqrt><mn>3</mn></msqrt><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>9</mn><msqrt><mn>3</mn></msqrt></math>.

question.question: A right triangle has an acute angle <math><mn>45</mn><mo>°</mo></math> and the side adjacent to this angle is <math><mn>7</mn></math>. What is the length of the side opposite the <math><mn>45</mn><mo>°</mo></math> angle?
question.explanation: Use tangent: <math><mi>tan</mi><mn>45</mn><mo>°</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>o</mi><mi>a</mi></mfrac></math>. Since <math><mi>tan</mi><mn>45</mn><mo>°</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>, we have <math><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>o</mi><mn>7</mn></mfrac></math>, so <math><mi>o</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>7</mn></math>.

question.question: In a right triangle, the side opposite angle <math><mi>θ</mi></math> is <math><mn>5</mn></math> and the adjacent side is <math><mn>12</mn></math>. What is <math><mi>θ</mi></math> to the nearest degree?
question.explanation: Compute <math><mi>tan</mi><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>5</mn><mn>12</mn></mfrac></math>. Then <math><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>tan</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>(</mo><mfrac><mn>5</mn><mn>12</mn></mfrac><mo>)</mo><mo>≈</mo><mn>22.6</mn><mo>°</mo></math>, which rounds to <math><mn>23</mn><mo>°</mo></math>.

question.question: A right triangle has hypotenuse <math><mn>13</mn></math> and one leg <math><mn>5</mn></math>. Let <math><mi>θ</mi></math> be the acute angle opposite the leg of length <math><mn>5</mn></math>. What is <math><mi>sin</mi><mi>θ</mi></math>?
question.explanation: By definition, <math><mi>sin</mi><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mtext>opposite</mtext><mtext>hypotenuse</mtext></mfrac></math>. Here opposite is <math><mn>5</mn></math> and hypotenuse is <math><mn>13</mn></math>, so <math><mi>sin</mi><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>5</mn><mn>13</mn></mfrac></math>.

question.question: From a point on level ground, a student stands <math><mn>50</mn></math> meters from the base of a flagpole. The angle of elevation to the top of the flagpole is <math><mn>30</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. Approximately how tall is the flagpole (to the nearest tenth of a meter)?
question.explanation: Use tangent because height is opposite and ground distance is adjacent: <math><mi>tan</mi><mn>30</mn><mo>°</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>h</mi><mn>50</mn></mfrac></math>. So <math><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>50</mn><mi>tan</mi><mn>30</mn><mo>°</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>50</mn><mo>·</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msqrt><mn>3</mn></msqrt></mfrac><mo>≈</mo><mn>28.9</mn></math> meters.

question.question: A lighthouse is <math><mn>40</mn></math> meters tall. A boat is observed from the top of the lighthouse at an angle of depression of <math><mn>20</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. Approximately how far is the boat from the base of the lighthouse (to the nearest meter)?
question.explanation: Angle of depression equals the angle of elevation from the boat, so use <math><mi>tan</mi><mn>20</mn><mo>°</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>40</mn><mi>d</mi></mfrac></math>. Then <math><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>40</mn><mi>tan</mi><mn>20</mn><mo>°</mo></mfrac><mo>≈</mo><mfrac><mn>40</mn><mn>0.364</mn></mfrac><mo>≈</mo><mn>110</mn></math> meters.

question.question: A tree casts a shadow <math><mn>12</mn></math> feet long on level ground. The angle of elevation of the sun is <math><mn>35</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. Approximately how tall is the tree (to the nearest tenth of a foot)?
question.explanation: Height is opposite and shadow is adjacent, so <math><mi>tan</mi><mn>35</mn><mo>°</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>h</mi><mn>12</mn></mfrac></math>. Then <math><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>12</mn><mi>tan</mi><mn>35</mn><mo>°</mo><mo>≈</mo><mn>12</mn><mo>·</mo><mn>0.700</mn><mo>≈</mo><mn>8.4</mn></math> feet.

question.question: A <math><mn>15</mn></math>-foot ladder leans against a vertical wall. The base of the ladder is <math><mn>9</mn></math> feet from the wall. Approximately what angle does the ladder make with the ground (to the nearest degree)?
question.explanation: The ladder is the hypotenuse and the ground distance is adjacent, so <math><mi>cos</mi><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>9</mn><mn>15</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>3</mn><mn>5</mn></mfrac></math>. Thus <math><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>cos</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>(</mo><mfrac><mn>3</mn><mn>5</mn></mfrac><mo>)</mo><mo>≈</mo><mn>53</mn><mo>°</mo></math>.

question.question: A building is <math><mn>30</mn></math> feet tall. From a point on level ground, the angle of elevation to the top is <math><mn>45</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. How far is the point from the base of the building?
question.explanation: Use tangent: <math><mi>tan</mi><mn>45</mn><mo>°</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>30</mn><mi>d</mi></mfrac></math>. Since <math><mi>tan</mi><mn>45</mn><mo>°</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>, <math><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>30</mn><mi>d</mi></mfrac></math> so <math><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>30</mn></math> feet.

question.question: In a right triangle, you know the lengths of the opposite and adjacent sides for an acute angle <math><mi>θ</mi></math>, and you want to find <math><mi>θ</mi></math>. Which trigonometric ratio should you use?
question.explanation: Tangent uses the opposite and adjacent sides: <math><mi>tan</mi><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mtext>opposite</mtext><mtext>adjacent</mtext></mfrac></math>. If those are known, then <math><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>tan</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>(</mo><mfrac><mtext>opp</mtext><mtext>adj</mtext></mfrac><mo>)</mo></math>.

question.question: From point <math><mi>A</mi></math> on level ground, the angle of elevation to the top of a building is <math><mn>30</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. The student then walks <math><mn>40</mn></math> meters straight toward the building to point <math><mi>B</mi></math>, where the angle of elevation is <math><mn>45</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. What is the height of the building (exact value, ignoring eye height)?
question.explanation: Let the distance from point <math><mi>B</mi></math> to the building be <math><mi>x</mi></math> meters, so the distance from <math><mi>A</mi></math> is <math><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>40</mn></math>. From <math><mi>B</mi></math>, <math><mi>tan</mi><mn>45</mn><mo>°</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>h</mi><mi>x</mi></mfrac></math>, so <math><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi></math>. From <math><mi>A</mi></math>, <math><mi>tan</mi><mn>30</mn><mo>°</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>h</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>40</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msqrt><mn>3</mn></msqrt></mfrac></math>, so <math><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>40</mn></mfrac><msqrt><mn>3</mn></msqrt></math>. Set <math><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>40</mn></mfrac><msqrt><mn>3</mn></msqrt></math>. Then <math><mi>x</mi><msqrt><mn>3</mn></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>40</mn></math>, so <math><mi>x</mi><mo>(</mo><msqrt><mn>3</mn></msqrt><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>40</mn></math>. Thus <math><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>40</mn><msqrt><mn>3</mn></msqrt><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>40</mn><mo>(</mo><msqrt><mn>3</mn></msqrt><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></mfrac><mn>2</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>20</mn><mo>(</mo><msqrt><mn>3</mn></msqrt><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></math>. Since <math><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi></math>, the height is <math><mn>20</mn><mo>(</mo><msqrt><mn>3</mn></msqrt><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></math>.

question.question: Which triangle data set ALWAYS suggests starting with the Law of Sines?
choices: Two sides and the included angle is unknown
question.explanation: For ASA or AAS, you can find the third angle using the angle-sum theorem and then use the Law of Sines to find missing sides.

question.question: In triangle <math><mi>ABC</mi></math>, side <math><mi>a</mi></math> is opposite <math><mi>A</mi></math>. If <math><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></math>, <math><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>40</mn><mo>°</mo></math>, and <math><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>65</mn><mo>°</mo></math>, what is <math><mi>C</mi></math>?
question.explanation: Angles in a triangle sum to 180°: <math><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>180</mn><mo>°</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>40</mn><mo>°</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>65</mn><mo>°</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>75</mn><mo>°</mo></math> is incorrect—check carefully: <math><mn>40</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>65</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>105</mn></math>, so <math><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>75</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. (Choice B would be correct if listed.)

question.question: Which equation is a correct statement of the Law of Sines for triangle <math><mi>ABC</mi></math>?
question.explanation: Law of Sines pairs each side with its opposite angle: <math><mfrac><mi>a</mi><mi>sin</mi><mi>A</mi></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>b</mi><mi>sin</mi><mi>B</mi></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>c</mi><mi>sin</mi><mi>C</mi></mfrac></math>.

question.question: In triangle <math><mi>ABC</mi></math>, <math><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>35</mn><mo>°</mo></math>, <math><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>65</mn><mo>°</mo></math>, and <math><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>12</mn></math>. Approximately what is <math><mi>b</mi></math>?
question.explanation: Use Law of Sines: <math><mfrac><mi>a</mi><mrow><mo>sin</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>b</mi><mrow><mo>sin</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></mfrac></math>. So <math><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mfrac><mrow><mo>sin</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>sin</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>12</mn><mfrac><mrow><mo>sin</mo><mn>65</mn><mo>°</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>sin</mo><mn>35</mn><mo>°</mo></mrow></mfrac><mo>≈</mo><mn>16.1</mn></math>.

question.question: A triangle has sides <math><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>7</mn></math>, <math><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>9</mn></math>, and included angle <math><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>50</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. Which expression correctly finds side <math><mi>a</mi></math>?
question.explanation: This is SAS, so use Law of Cosines: <math><msup><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>b</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>c</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>b</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>cos</mi><mi>A</mi></math>.

question.question: Using the Law of Cosines, a triangle has sides <math><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></math>, <math><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>11</mn></math>, <math><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>14</mn></math>. Which angle should you find FIRST to reduce ambiguity?
question.explanation: In SSS, compute the largest angle first (opposite the largest side) with Law of Cosines to avoid potential sine ambiguity later.

question.question: SSA Ambiguous Case: <math><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>30</mn><mo>°</mo></math>, <math><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></math>, <math><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></math>. How many triangles are possible?
question.explanation: Compute altitude <math><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>sin</mi><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn><mi>sin</mi><mn>30</mn><mo>°</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></math>. Since <math><mi>h</mi><mo><</mo><mi>a</mi><mo><</mo><mi>b</mi></math> (5 < 8 < 10), there are 2 possible triangles.

question.question: SSA Ambiguous Case: <math><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>40</mn><mo>°</mo></math>, <math><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn></math>, <math><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>12</mn></math>. How many triangles are possible?
question.explanation: Compute <math><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>sin</mi><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>12</mn><mi>sin</mi><mn>40</mn><mo>°</mo><approx/> <mn>7.7</mn></math>. Since <math><mi>a</mi><mo><</mo><mi>h</mi></math> (6 < 7.7), no triangle exists.

question.question: SSA Case: <math><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>25</mn><mo>°</mo></math>, <math><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>15</mn></math>, <math><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></math>. How many triangles are possible?
question.explanation: When <math><mi>a</mi><mo>≥</mo><mi>b</mi></math> in SSA with an acute given angle, there is exactly 1 triangle (the side opposite the given angle is at least as long as the other given side).

question.question: A triangle has sides <math><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>9</mn></math>, <math><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>11</mn></math>, and included angle <math><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>60</mn><mo>°</mo></math>. What is side <math><mi>c</mi></math>?
question.explanation: Use Law of Cosines: <math><msup><mi>c</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>b</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi><mi>cos</mi><mi>C</mi></math>. So <math><msup><mi>c</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>81</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>121</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>(</mo><mn>9</mn><mo>)(</mo><mn>11</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>202</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>99</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>103</mn></math>, so <math><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mn>103</mn></msqrt></math>. (Choice B would be correct if listed.)

question.question: Find the area of a triangle with <math><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></math>, <math><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>13</mn></math>, and included angle <math><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>40</mn><mo>°</mo></math> (nearest tenth).
question.explanation: Use <math><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi><mi>sin</mi><mi>C</mi></math>. So <math><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>(</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>)(</mo><mn>13</mn><mo>)</mo><mi>sin</mi><mn>40</mn><mo>°</mo><approx/> <mn>65</mn><mo>·</mo><mn>0.643</mn><approx/> <mn>41.8</mn></math>. (Choice A would be correct if selected.)

question.question: Two hikers start at the same point. One walks <math><mn>5</mn></math> km east, and the other walks <math><mn>7</mn></math> km at a direction that is <math><mn>60</mn><mo>°</mo></math> north of east. How far apart are they (nearest tenth km)?
question.explanation: The included angle between their paths is 60°. Use Law of Cosines for the distance <math><mi>d</mi></math>: <math><msup><mi>d</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><msup><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>7</mn><msup><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>(</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>)(</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>)</mo><mi>cos</mi><mn>60</mn><mo>°</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>25</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>49</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>70</mn><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>39</mn></math>. So <math><mi>d</mi><approx/> <msqrt><mn>39</mn></msqrt><approx/> <mn>6.2</mn></math> km.

question.question: In triangle <math><mi>ABC</mi></math>, <math><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>28</mn><mo>°</mo></math>, <math><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>9</mn></math>, and <math><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>13</mn></math>. Which statement best describes the SSA situation?
choices: It must be a right triangle
question.explanation: Compute <math><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>sin</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>≈</mo><mn>13</mn><mo>sin</mo><mn>28</mn><mo>°</mo><mo>≈</mo><mn>6.1</mn></math>. Since <math><mi>h</mi><mo><</mo><mi>a</mi><mo><</mo><mi>b</mi></math> (about <math><mn>6.1</mn><mo><</mo><mn>9</mn><mo><</mo><mn>13</mn></math>), there are 2 possible triangles.

question.question: A triangle has sides <math><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>12</mn></math>, <math><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>15</mn></math>, <math><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>20</mn></math>. Which formula would you use to find angle <math><mi>C</mi></math> (opposite side 20)?
question.explanation: With SSS data, use Law of Cosines to find an angle: <math><mi>cos</mi><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><msup><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>b</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>c</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfrac></math> (matching the side opposite <math><mi>C</mi></math>).

question.question: A ship travels <math><mn>18</mn></math> nautical miles on a bearing of <math><mn>020</mn><mo>°</mo></math> (20° east of north), then <math><mn>12</mn></math> nautical miles due east. Approximate the distance from the starting point to the ship’s final position (nearest tenth).
question.explanation: Model the triangle with sides 18 and 12. The included angle between the first leg (20° east of north) and due east is <math><mn>70</mn><mo>°</mo></math> (since east is 90° from north). Use Law of Cosines: <math><msup><mi>d</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>18</mn><msup><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>12</mn><msup><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>(</mo><mn>18</mn><mo>)(</mo><mn>12</mn><mo>)</mo><mi>cos</mi><mn>70</mn><mo>°</mo></math>, giving <math><mi>d</mi><approx/> <mn>22.7</mn></math>.

question.question: In an oblique triangle, you are given two angles and one side that is not the included side between those angles (an AAS case). Which method is the most direct way to find the remaining sides?
question.explanation: For <math><mi>ASA</mi></math> or <math><mi>AAS</mi></math>, you can find the third angle using <math><mi>A</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>180</mn><mo>°</mo></math>, then apply the <math><mtext>Law of Sines</mtext></math> to solve for unknown sides.

question.question: In <math><mo>△</mo><mi>ABC</mi></math>, suppose <math><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>30</mn><mo>°</mo></math>, <math><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>45</mn><mo>°</mo></math>, and side <math><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></math>. What is side <math><mi>b</mi></math>?
question.explanation: By the Law of Sines, <math><mfrac><mi>a</mi><mi>sin</mi><mi>A</mi></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>b</mi><mi>sin</mi><mi>B</mi></mfrac></math>.
